title: UPID — Universal Personal Identity: A conceptual framework for biometrically anchored, federated personhood without central data storage
abstract: This whitepaper sets out a conceptual framework for a global personhoodsystem (UPID — Universal Personal Identity) that avoids the centralstructural weaknesses of the approaches discussed to date — fromWorldcoin through the European Digital Identity Wallet to social-graphprocedures. The framework rests on three choices: a reduction of the problem fieldto two viable core problems (uniqueness at enrolment and continuity onreturn); a strict separation between an attribute-free personhood layerand an application-specific application layer; and a resolution of thetrilemma global · deduplicated · without central data storage through afederated existential query. From these choices, thirteen core requirements (A1–A13) are derived thatdescribe the framework conclusively. Six explicit non-requirements keepquestions out of the core that could not be answered at system levelwithout violating fundamental rights. A two-tier application model with tiered attributes enables both purepersonhood applications and name-bound applications, including use as afully-fledged passport system under ICAO 9303. Concrete cryptographic procedures and protocol details are deliberatelyoutside this document and are the subject of separate work. This textserves to fix authorship of the framework described as of the date ofits publication. In case of interpretive doubt, the German original v1.0is authoritative.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Mind Uploading and Consciousness Replication: A Typed Ladder for State Capture, Functional Equivalence, Causal Continuity, and Personal Identity
abstract: # Provider Description Mind uploading is often treated as a single achievement, but a measured connectome, a runnable reconstruction, behavioral similarity, causal continuity, consciousness, and personal identity are different claims. This paper develops a typed evidence ladder that keeps those claims separate and specifies what evidence would be needed at each rung. The paper introduces an executable Upload Ladder Benchmark for testing artificial source agents and reconstructions under controlled state capture, body transfer, branching, perturbation, held-out tasks, and matched baselines. Two synthetic study families reach different local conclusions, so their results remain stratified rather than pooled. All adverse, null, censored, and failed-intervention records remain part of the evidence surface. A machine-checked Lean 4 layer verifies narrow decision, custody, censorship, revocation, rollback, and fission invariants without claiming to formalize a brain or settle consciousness or identity. The release includes the manuscript, five figures, a claim-source matrix, a strongest-form challenge register, validation records, and a reproducibility archive containing code, configurations, tests, checkpoints, score ledgers, and formal-proof receipts. The biological final-test plan remains sealed and unopened. The reported results are synthetic engineering evidence only; they do not establish biological mind uploading, replicated consciousness, numerical personal identity, personal continuity, or human feasibility. ## Keywords mind uploading; whole-brain emulation; Self-Aware Networks; connectomics; state sufficiency; functional equivalence; causal continuity; consciousness; personal identity; reproducibility

title: UPID — Universal Personal Identity: Ein konzeptioneller Rahmen für biometrisch verankerte, föderierte Personhood ohne zentrale Datenspeicherung
abstract: Dieses Whitepaper stellt einen konzeptionellen Rahmen für ein globalesPersonhood-System (UPID — Universal Personal Identity) vor, das diezentralen strukturellen Schwächen der bisher diskutierten Ansätze — vonWorldcoin über die European Digital Identity Wallet bis zu Social-Graph-Verfahren — vermeidet. Der Rahmen beruht auf drei Entscheidungen: einer Reduktion des Problemfeldsauf zwei tragfähige Kernprobleme (Uniqueness bei Anlage und Continuity beiRückkehr); einer strikten Trennung zwischen einem attributfreienPersonhood-Layer und einem anwendungsspezifischen Applikations-Layer; undder Auflösung des Trilemmas global · dedupliziert · ohne zentraleDatenspeicherung durch eine föderierte Existenzabfrage. Aus diesen Entscheidungen werden dreizehn Kernanforderungen (A1–A13)abgeleitet, die den Rahmen abschließend beschreiben. Sechs expliziteNicht-Anforderungen halten Fragen aus dem Kern heraus, die aufSystemebene nicht ohne Verletzung fundamentaler Rechte beantwortbar wären. Ein zweischichtiges Anwendungsmodell mit gestuften Attributen erschließtsowohl reine Personhood-Anwendungen als auch namensgebundene Anwendungeneinschließlich der Nutzung als vollwertiges Passsystem nach ICAO 9303. title: Legal Analysis of Name Change as a Form of Personal Identity Protection: A Case Study of District Court Decision Number 196/Pdt.P/2024/PN Jbg
abstract: Name change constitutes an important legal mechanism within Indonesia's population administration system to ensure the consistency and legal validity of personal identity recorded in official documents. However, inconsistencies in identity data caused by differences in name spelling, historical recording errors, and undocumented name changes continue to create legal uncertainty and administrative obstacles, as reflected in District Court Decision Number 196/Pdt.P/2024/PN Jbg. This study aims to analyze the judge's legal considerations in granting the application for a name change and to examine the role of name change as a form of legal protection for personal identity. This research employs a normative legal research method using statutory, conceptual, and case approaches, supported by primary and secondary legal materials analyzed through qualitative methods. The findings indicate that the court granted the application after the applicant successfully proved inconsistencies in identity data across several official documents and demonstrated that the requested name change did not violate statutory provisions or public interests. The court's decision was based on documentary evidence, witness testimony, and the applicable population administration laws. Furthermore, the decision confirms that a court-approved name change provides legal certainty, harmonizes population administration records, strengthens legal recognition of an individual's identity, and facilitates access to public administrative services. Therefore, a judicial determination of a name change functions not only as an administrative correction but also as an effective legal instrument for protecting personal identity and ensuring legal certainty within Indonesia's population administration system.
venue: JIHAD Jurnal Ilmu Hukum dan Administrasi

title: Intelligenza artificiale e diritto all’identità personale: sfide e potenzialità
abstract: This paper examines some possible critical issues arising from the development of artificial intelligence systems with regard to the protection of the right to personal identity. After attempting to provide a definition of the right to personal identity, the analysis will focus on two particular applications of artificial intelligence that can severly undermine the exercise of this right, namely deep fake content and the use of remote biometric identification systems in public spaces (analysing, specifically, their use in the Hungarian context). This is particularly relevant today, not only because of the rapid technological development we are witnessing, but also in light of recent legislative measures adopted within the European Union. Finally, the virtual dimension of personal identity will be considered, seeking to examine the problems and potential inherent in recognising a right to digital identity.

title: The seed hypothesis
abstract: This hypothesis proposes that the person we become is shaped by an interaction between our initial biological conditions, our environment, the experiences we accumulate, the memories we retain, and the meanings we assign to those experiences. It explores what this could mean for personal identity, personality, free will, cultural evolution, and ultimately consciousness.

title: The effect of social identity on objective and perceived social support in groups
abstract: The social identity approach posits that social identity fosters mutual social support within groups. However, prior research has relied almost exclusively on individual-level self-report measures, neglecting the mutuality of support and the group as a unit of analysis. This pre-registered one-factorial online experiment with three-person groups (N = 306 group members; N = 102 groups) examined how social identity shapes objective mutual support, perceived provided and received support and the perceived benevolence of received support. Following a pre-tested identity manipulation (N = 120), groups completed a video-recorded workplace simulation. Transcripts were blind-coded. Groups in the social identity condition engaged in significantly more objective mutual social support than participants in the personal identity condition. Social identity (vs. personal identity) did not affect perceived support but increased perceived benevolence, in terms of assuming underlying motives. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing among objective mutual social support at the group-level, perceived social support and the interpretation of social support to understand how shared social identity shapes the social support process.

title: Potret Kecenderungan Penggunaan Hijab Mahasiswi Gen Z di Kampus IAIN Fattahul Muluk Papua
abstract: The purpose of this study is to describe and analyze the phenomenon of hijab usage trends among Generation Z female students at IAIN Fattahul Muluk Papua. Specifically, it examines how hijab styles are adopted by students, the factors influencing these tendencies, and how they interpret and construct the meaning of wearing the hijab amid rapidly evolving fashion currents. This research employs a qualitative descriptive approach. Data were collected through observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation. The data were analyzed using a flow model of qualitative analysis. The findings indicate that the hijab styles of Generation Z female students at IAIN Fattahul Muluk Papua reflect contemporary dynamics of religious and social identity. The hijab functions not merely as attire, but as a symbol constructed through the interaction between personal identity, collective norms, digital media, and campus culture. Preferences for minimalist designs and neutral colors demonstrate the influence of youth habitus and modern visual culture. Although social media and globalization provide strong stylistic inspiration, students selectively adapt these influences to align with norms of modesty and Islamic principles (sharia). Overall, hijab fashion among these students represents a process of negotiation between global trends, personal identity, Islamic values, and the socio-cultural structure of the campus environment.
venue: SOSMANIORA Jurnal Ilmu Sosial dan Humaniora

title: International Journal of Information Technology Project Management
abstract: This article reports what information members of a virtual project team specifically find important for the formation of an initial impression of the trustworthiness of their colleagues.Collaboration in virtual project teams heavily relies on interpersonal trust, for which perceived trustworthiness is an important determinant.We reviewed different trust-requiring and collaborative online environments to determine what information people have available through profiles.Taking this analysis as a starting point, a group of 226 students with experience in virtual project teams was questioned on signals they preferred to use to form an impression of trustworthiness.On the basis of the results obtained we have formulated several recommendations for the design of groupware environments.They pertain in particular to personal identity profiles.
venue: International Journal of Information Technology Project Management

title: What we talk to when we talk to language models
abstract: When we talk to large language models, who or what is our interlocutor? First, I address some issues about how best to characterize the interlocutor in terms of mental states. Second, I discuss questions in the philosophy of computation about what sort of AI system an LLM interlocutor might be: a model, an instance, a thread, or a persona? Third, I analyze some issues about personal identity in LLM interlocutors. Fourth, I draw some conclusions about issues of AI welfare and moral status.
topic: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: THE NEW BABEL BUILDERS Artificial Intelligence and the Crisis of Human Centrality
abstract: This paper investigates the philosophical crisis arising from advances in Artificial Intelligence, moving beyond functional debates about machine automation and human replacement. It introduces the concept of "algorithmic anthropological reduction" to describe how measurable human capabilities are progressively transformed into implicit metrics of human worth. Drawing on philosophy of mind, philosophy of technology, and theories of personal identity, the article argues that defending human dignity in the algorithmic age requires rejecting the reduction of human value to optimizable performance metrics, calling instead for a reconstruction of human centrality rooted in normative agency and shared forms of life.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
topic: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: FACEBOOK CONFESSION STUDY - DATASET
abstract: The corpus consisted of 10169 words extracted from a total of 120 posts written entirely in Vietnamese. The confessions were submitted anonymously so students are likely to be more straightforward (Babari, 2015) when presenting an issue or raising concerns, knowing that their personal identity is protected. To ensure anonymity and privacy, no personal information was collected or included in the analysis. Additionally, any potentially identifying information (e.g. names or locations), was redacted to maintain anonymity. Furthermore, strict adherence to data protection regulations was followed, and necessary permissions were obtained from the page administrators before accessing and analyzing the data.

title: Repetition and Stability within Human Temporality: An Existential-Phenomenological Approach
abstract: This article develops a threefold model of human temporality—ecstatic-horizontal, cyclical-repetitive, and linear-irreversible—by integrating insights from Heideggerian phenomenology, embodiment theory, and contemporary phenomenological research. Emphasizing the role of repetition across all three dimensions, the article explores how temporal structure contributes to the formation and stability of personal identity. Special attention is given to the interplay between consciousness and embodiment, and to the existential implications of finitude. Repetition emerges not as mere recurrence, but as a constitutive act, at times taking on a rhythmic character, through which authenticity, continuity, and self-understanding are enacted within time.

title: Topological and Spectral Consistency of Mind Uploading via Univalent Rough Operator Algebra (UROA)
abstract: This paper formalizes the theoretical mechanisms of Mind Uploading (Whole Brain Emulation) through the lens of Univalent Rough Operator Algebra (UROA) [5] and Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT) [6]. We define biological consciousness as a persistent spectral invariant of a neural connectome graph. By distinguishing the ”Copy” method from the ”Gradual Transfer” method, we mathematically prove that while copying results in topological bifurcation (identity loss), gradual transfer constitutes a valid homotopy continuation in the ROA space, thereby strictly preserving personal identity. A Python-based spectral graphsimulation is provided as a constructive computational proof.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Collective Latent States Across Generations: A Typed Formal Model and Terminal Audit (BIT-LMIND-COLLECTIVE-LATENT-001)
abstract: This archival technical release presents a typed, model-internal framework for collective latent states across collective lineages, cohorts, individuals, carriers, channels, traces and environments. It formalizes uptake, deposit, reenactment, selection, forgetting and reactivation while preserving strict non-identity and claim-ceiling controls. The F4 formal target was positive only within the frozen model; F5 terminal closure added no new proof, repair, theorem, empirical run, authority or effect. This release does not establish collective consciousness, inherited personal identity, a metaphysical collective unconscious, a biological mechanism, empirical validity, independent replication or public truth.

title: Digital Communication Among Generation Z Students: an Integrated Perspective from the University of Warsaw
abstract: Digital communication has become an integral component of Generation Z’s everyday life, influencing interpersonal interaction, learning, relationship maintenance, and identity expression. Previous research has explored different aspects of Generation Z’s digital communication. The aim of this study is to examine Generation Z students’ digital communication from an integrated perspective encompassing three interconnected dimensions: communication intensity, communication practices, and communication culture. The research employed a quantitative cross-sectional survey based on an anonymous online questionnaire completed by 133 students enrolled at the University of Warsaw. The questionnaire included closed-ended items addressing the frequency of social media and messaging application use, preferred platforms and communication formats, attitudes toward video calls, voice messages, and delayed responses, as well as perceptions of online friendships, public self-expression, and the importance of personal identity in digital environments. The results confirm the central role of digital communication in students’ everyday lives. Social media and messaging applications were identified as the principal channels of interaction, while respondents demonstrated flexibility in selecting platforms and communication forms according to situational needs. The findings further revealed broad acceptance of delayed responses, selective use of voice messages, and generally positive attitudes toward video-mediated communication. Most participants regarded online friendships as meaningful relationships while continuing to value face-to-face interaction. Although personal identity was considered important by the majority of respondents, relatively few expressed their personal views publicly online, reflecting a selective and context-dependent approach to digital participation. The study provides an integrated perspective on Generation Z’s digital communication and contributes to a better understanding of communication behaviour in contemporary digital environments.

title: BIT-COG-001-R0 — Hierarchical Retentive Assembly and Bounded Verification: Master Overview, Claim Boundary, Reproduction Guide and Independent Research Handoff
abstract: BIT-COG-001-R0 is the independent-research handoff release of the Boundary Information Theory memory and consciousness-claim-boundary program through F5R1. It converts an early conceptual lineage—boundary observers, self-reference, transformed perception, embodied brain-heart coupling, historical memory, causal obligations and possible cross-death continuity—into a typed and scope-limited research architecture. The release formalizes Hierarchical Retentive Assembly (HRA): stable components are not sufficient for memory. A candidate memory domain additionally requires historically discriminative retention, renewal invariance, cross-scale readout, decoding and causal re-entry. The architecture separates material persistence, organizational continuity, phenomenal consciousness, personal identity, causal debt and cross-death continuity. The analytic layer contains a locked proof DAG with 31 nodes and 37 edges. The bounded executable layer records 14/14 active test lanes, 12/12 replay records, 4/4 exact-arithmetic traces, 35/35 active proof/certificate checks, 8/8 guard controls and two byte-identical clean runs. The F5R1 verdict is KERNEL_CHECKED within the frozen finite slate. Scope boundary: this release does not establish a universal theorem, does not empirically validate ERBS, does not solve the physical-to-phenomenal bridge and does not prove personal identity across death or reincarnation. Cross-death continuity remains HOLD pending an explicit carrier, encoding, survival boundary, transport route, decoder, identity invariant and discriminating prediction. The deposit includes the master handoff report, active F0–F5R1 formal lineage, F4R2 analytic proof artifact, F5R1 verification dossier, cryptographic checksums and a reproducibility package.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Conservation Hypothesis.
abstract: This paper examines the plausibility, though not the proof, of a hypothesis that consciousness may be tied to a form of energy that persists beyond biological death. The argument proceeds from an established physical premise, the conservation of energy, through a contested but serious philosophical position, panpsychism, and into the empirical territory of near-death experience research, before arriving at an honest accounting of where the hypothesis is well supported, where it is speculative, and where it currently has no supporting mechanism at all. The paper does not claim to prove survival of personal identity after death. It instead attempts to isolate which parts of that claim rest on solid ground and which parts remain, at present, unanswered questions rather than established facts.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Probabilistic Horizon of Immortality: The Statistical Survival Limit of a Biological Substrate under Eliminated Senescence
abstract: This paper re-evaluates the actuarial consequences of eliminated senescence, deriving a constant-hazard survival distribution with a finite mean and a vanishing tail probability over millennial horizons. Extending the analysis to astroengineering and cosmological scales, it demonstrates the quantitative irrelevance of the biological substrate for multi-million-year trajectories. The two candidate strategies for circumventing this finite ceiling—environmental risk suppression and substrate migration—are examined. Thermodynamic constraints are argued to preclude the former, as a zero-hazard limit is incompatible with the permanent development required in a degrading universe, thereby identifying the copyable, redundant architecture as the necessary condition for continued persistence. This conclusion is qualified by its dependence on the structural criterion of personal identity, presented as an unresolved epistemic contingency rather than a settled assumption.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Neurorights in the Age of Neurotechnology and Digital Health. Are New Rights Necessary to Protect the Mind?
abstract: The present paper is concerned with the ongoing debate on neurorights from the standpoint of legal philosophy. The fundamental question is whether these rights should be understood as a reinterpretation of existing fundamental rights or as a distinct emerging legal category. Methodologically, the paper combines conceptual analysis, comparative law and the study of international soft law instruments in order to assess the legal status and practical function of neurorights. It then analyses their ethical and normative foundations, placing particular emphasis on human dignity, personal autonomy, mental privacy, mental integrity and personal identity. Furthermore, it explores their legal ramifications within the framework of comparative law, international soft law and digital health. In this realm, the collection, processing and interpretation of neurodata give rise to the question of whether conventional legal safeguards remain sufficient.
venue: The Age of Human Rights Journal

title: Asleep Until the Resurrection? Soul Sleep, Consciousness, and the Limits of Biblical Inference
abstract: This article examines whether biblical descriptions of death as sleep imply unconsciousness until the resurrection. Through close readings of Ecclesiastes, Daniel, John, Paul’s letters, Luke, and Revelation, it considers the strongest arguments for soul sleep and conscious fellowship with Christ after death. Historical discussion draws on Irenaeus, Calvin’s Psychopannychia, the Westminster Confession, and Seventh-day Adventist teaching. The article argues that sleep language alone does not establish unconsciousness. Several New Testament passages provide substantial grounds for conscious fellowship with Christ, although they leave the nature of that experience largely unexplained. Bodily resurrection remains central to Christian hope. The discussion also considers personal identity, the experience of time, and responsible pastoral language about death and grief.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: National identity, common civic creed and religious conflict in Latin America
abstract: The social cohesion of many societies may depend, among other factors, on the affirmation of a common civic creed. In this regard, one of the most relevant questions is why some societies have succeeded in building a sense of national identity associated with civic values, while other societies have not. To answer this question, I propose a heuristic model of the nation as family and postulate that several of the mechanisms that help explain national identity formation are similar to the mechanisms that contribute to explain personal identity formation. Based on this model, I show that the church-state conflict has been decisive in the formation of national identity in Latin America and present evidence from four countries about the effect of this conflict on the levels observed support for democracy, obedience to the law, spread of violence and corruption, as manifestations of quite different configurations of national identity.
topic: Religion and Society in Latin America

title: IDENTITÀ E VULNERABILITÀ NELL’ECOSISTEMA DIGITALE. IL CASO DELLA TUTELA DEI MINORI NELL’USO DEI DISPOSITIVI DI INTELLIGENZA ARTIFICIALE CONVERSAZIONALE
abstract: In cyberspace, an individual's identity profile is increasingly determined by external choices, with the risk of being exploited, adulterated, and even falsified without the possibility of effective opposition. Cyberspace is progressively redrawing the relationship between personal autonomy and identity, making it necessary to develop new tools for protection, not only of a legal nature but above all of a cultural and social nature. The position of minors in the digital world is even more complex, as they, especially in early childhood, are at a stage of life where their personal identity is still being formed and constructed. There is a clear need to explore new avenues to fully protect children's identities, ranging from greater awareness among those exercising parental responsibility to greater regulatory protection for children in the face of the development of devices such as chatbots and forms of conversational and generative AI.

title: BÀN VỀ VẤN ĐỀ XÁC MINH TRONG CÔNG CHỨNG GIAO DỊCH - THỰC TRẠNG VÀ GIẢI PHÁP
abstract: Verification is an essential professional responsibility of notaries in ensuring the authenticity and legality of civil transactions.In notarial practice, verification has become increasingly important because of the growing prevalence of forged documents, fraudulent conduct in real estate transactions, and difficulties in determining legal capacity, personal identity, and the legal status of assets involved in transactions.Nevertheless, current verification practices remain subject to several limitations, including the absence of uniform regulations governing verification procedures and ineffective mechanisms for coordination and information sharing.Based on an analysis of relevant legal provisions, their practical implementation, and the experience of France, this article proposes measures to improve the legal framework by standardizing verification procedures, enhancing access to and utilization of databases, and strengthening coordination mechanisms in notarial practice.These measures are intended to improve legal certainty and safeguard civil transactions in the context of digital transformation.

title: Influencia de la moda y las redes sociales en las decisiones consumistas de los jóvenes
abstract: The present essay analyzes the influence of fashion and social media on young people’s consumer decisions, with the purpose of explaining the psychological, social, and historical factors involved in this phenomenon. It is argued that the dissemination of fashion-related content through social media influences young people’s consumer decisions by being closely linked to the search for personal identity and the need for social validation. To support this argument, the essay integrates a theoretical framework complemented by an exploratory survey conducted with 28 young participants. The results show that TikTok and Instagram exert the greatest influence on the dissemination of fashion trends, encouraging impulsive purchases, and strengthen social comparison and the pursuit of acceptance. Overall, the findings support the proposed thesis and highlight self-awareness as a fundamental tool for promoting more conscious, critical, and responsible consumer decisions.

title: The Mystery of Marriage – Communion, Creation and Fulfillment in Christ
abstract: This study explores the Mystery of Marriage as a dynamic reality of communion, creation, and fulfillment in Christ. Grounded in the divine model of Trinitarian love, marriage is presented as a sacred union that transfigures human relationships and reveals their ultimate meaning in God. The work examines marriage as an icon of the mystical union between the soul and God, as well as a manifestation of Trinitarian communion within human existence. It highlights the Christian family as the ‘church at home,’ the primary space where loneliness is overcome, and personal identity is fulfilled through love and self giving. The study also analyses the family as a place of creative love and the realization of human vocation, while addressing the contemporary crisis of divorce as a rupture of communion and a distortion of the family’s spiritual calling. The conclusions affirm that Christian marriage is not merely a social institution but a path to holiness, mutual sacrifice, and cooperation with God, where love becomes incarnate and fruitful in the life of the family.

title: The Learning Loop That Learns Itself: From Recursive Self-Reference to Phase-Compatible Self-World Reinstatement in Self-Aware Networks
abstract: This preprint distinguishes recursive self-reference, learned self-models, embodied learning-loop closure, and conscious self-world rendering. It reconstructs the dated SAN genealogy; connects action-feedback, proprioception, the Gamma Consideration Sandwich, phase-wave differentials, and Artificial Neurology; specifies a causal and mathematical model; reports two frozen synthetic development studies; and provides a bounded Lean verification layer. The evidence is mixed and explicitly does not establish biological consciousness, phase necessity, or SAN-specific algorithmic superiority. ## Evidence boundary The application evidence is deterministic and synthetic. Lean verifies only the declared finite interface, accounting, custody, and claim-boundary invariants. Neither layer establishes biological consciousness, artificial sentience, the complete GCS architecture, phase necessity, personal identity, or SAN-specific superiority. The manuscript is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Boundary Between Change and Identity: A Conceptual Framework on Personal Continuity and Recurrent Behavioral Patterns
abstract: This research document introduces a multidisciplinary conceptual framework investigating the fundamental relationship between personal identity, personality dynamics, and recurrent behavioral patterns. Originating from the "Duluktz System" framework, the paper challenges the traditional view of personality as a static essence, redefining it as a dynamic system of learned traits, habits, and cognitive feedback loops. The study proposes a novel, multidimensional "Identity Continuity Index" (ICI) that separates personal persistence from mere psychological similarity across time, decomposing identity into four distinct analytical levels: biological, psychological, narrative, and behavioral continuity. Furthermore, the framework outlines testable experimental designs to explore self-concept shifts and cognitive reframing, incorporates contemporary longitudinal literature in personality science, and establishes rigorous falsifiability criteria to refine longstanding philosophical and behavioral debates on continuity through transformation.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Who am I?: Introduction to partition theory
abstract: This text presents a didactic introduction to partition theory, explaining that a partition is the decomposition of a positive integer into a sum of other positive integers, regardless of order, and provides examples for small values of n. Through a dialogue between two teenagers, Sergio and Rocío, and their mysterious professor Laripse, a philosophical analogy is drawn between numerical partitions and personal identity, understood as the sum of social interactions. The material then develops pedagogical methods for calculating partitions with restrictions (using only certain summands, such as 1 and 2, or 1, 2, and 3), introduces the concept of a "fixed number" or generating partition to approximate values of P(n), and proposes five practical activities for students to experience the difficulty of manual counting, reinforce recursive patterns, and develop an operational understanding without resorting to complex formulas such as Euler's generating function or the Hardy-Ramanujan asymptotic formula.

title: The Ethics of Dialogue in Paul Ricœur: A Philosophical Analysis in Light of Hermeneutic Thought and Identity
abstract: This study explores the ethics of dialogue in Paul Ricœur's philosophy within the framework of hermeneutic thought and narrative identity. It argues that dialogue is not merely a communicative act or a linguistic exchange but an ethical and existential process through which the self is constituted, interpreted, and transformed in relation to the other. The research examines the fundamental dimensions of Ricœur’s conception of dialogue, including recognition, plurality, moral imagination, responsibility, and institutional justice. It demonstrates that ethical dialogue depends on the ability to acknowledge difference, engage in mutual understanding, and establish relationships based on respect and responsibility. Furthermore, the study highlights the role of narrative identity in shaping the relationship between self and other, showing that personal identity emerges through interpretation, memory, and interaction. It concludes that Ricœur’s philosophy provides a valuable ethical model for promoting coexistence, reconciliation, and meaningful communication in contemporary societies characterised by cultural diversity and moral plurality.

title: UNIVERSAL VALUES OF WORLD LITERATURE IN THE ERA OF GLOBAL TRANSFORMATIONS
abstract: The contemporary world is experiencing profound social, cultural, and technological transformations that reshape systems of values and redefine the foundations of human coexistence. Under these conditions, world literature acquires renewed significance as a universal cultural phenomenon capable of preserving and transmitting ethical ideals across historical periods and national boundaries. This study examines the role of world literature in the formation of universal human values from a social philosophical and axiological perspective. The paper argues that literary texts perform not merely aesthetic functions but also serve as instruments of moral cognition, intercultural communication, and spiritual continuity. Special attention is devoted to the humanistic traditions embodied in classical and modern literary works and their influence on the development of personal identity, civic consciousness, and intercultural dialogue. The findings demonstrate that world literature remains one of the most effective cultural mechanisms for preserving humanistic ideals in the context of globalization and digital transformation.

title: Linguistic legacies: a testimonio of how mentorship shapes multilingual faculty in a US context
abstract: This article presents three testimonios that center the lived experiences of women whose paths intersected across language, identity, mentorship, and higher education. Through our collective voices, we highlight the transformative influence of mentorship and institutional support in shaping the trajectories of multilingual educators in higher education. We examine how bilingualism, advocacy, and mentorship became not only professional assets but also catalysts that created opportunities previously considered unattainable. Our narratives address cultural and linguistic barriers, the tension between institutional expectations and personal identity, and the distinct challenges encountered by multilingual faculty and leaders in academic contexts. Collectively, our testimonios honor the journeys that brought us to this point and illuminate a path for those who may identify with our stories; as educators, advocates, and individuals who rightfully belong in every academic space they choose to enter.

title: The Disrupted Rhythms of Life and the Philosophy of Kata in Japanese Film
abstract: This article examines disruptions in life’s rhythms and the processes through which harmony is restored in two Japanese films: Tokyo Sonata (2008) by Kurosawa Kiyoshi and Happy Family Plan (2000) by Abe Tsutomu. Bringing Henri Lefebvre’s rhythmanalysis into dialogue with the Japanese philosophical concept of kata, the study argues that both films mobilize a logic akin to kata, wherein identity is defined through the patterned repetition of everyday practices and socially constituted roles, negotiated through moments of disruption. Music, particularly piano lessons and recurring chords, functions as a medium of disturbance and reconfiguration of kata-like rhythms. The analysis demonstrates that rhythm and kata converge in their emphasis on repetition and rupture while differing in origin and ontological grounding. Reconceptualizing kata as a historically responsive, embodied practice central to personal identity, this article contributes to film, cultural, and philosophical debates on rhythm and self-formation.

title: Neurotecnologie e sicurezza cognitiva nella dinamica tra individuo e Stato
abstract: In the neurotechnological era, the convergence of mind-intervention techniques and artificial intelligence systems poses simultaneous risks to both individual cognitive security and State security. Techniques that record, modulate, or alter neural activity – thereby influencing thought formation and extracting information – ultimately undermine personal identity, the inviolable core of the individual, as well as the capacity for autonomous self-determination. When such interventions target the political will or the minds of individuals holding high-level decision-making roles or compromise the confidentiality of the information known to them, the impact extends beyond the personal sphere. Accordingly, they pose, respectively, a threat to popular sovereignty and democratic legitimacy on the one hand, and to strategic interests and national stability on the other. This article advocates a systemic understanding of the link between individual neurointegrity and institutional resilience, emphasizing the need for multi‑layered protection of neurorights and, in particular, for the safeguarding of mental integrity as a foundational prerequisite for the endurance of democratic systems.

title: Technology Matters: Using digital mental health tools for children and young people – clinical implications of neurorights
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital mental health technologies is transforming child and adolescent mental health services through tools such as wearable devices, behavioural monitoring, predictive algorithms and digital interventions. While these innovations offer opportunities for earlier detection, personalised care and improved continuity of support, they also raise important ethical and developmental challenges. Current neurorights frameworks have emerged to protect mental privacy, autonomy, personal identity and agency in response to advances in neuroscience and neurotechnology. However, these frameworks have largely been developed with adults in mind and may not adequately address the distinctive vulnerabilities of children and adolescents. This article examines the implications of digital mental health technologies in young people from a developmental neurorights perspective. It argues that safeguarding children's rights means keeping open the possibilities for their development, avoiding labelling or categorising them too early and respecting their growing autonomy. Clinical, service and policy recommendations are proposed to support ethically responsible implementation.

title: Memdeklaro: Self-Declared Identity as an Identity Issuer of Last Resort
abstract: Modern societies increasingly rely on government-issued identity documents to establish access to employment, housing, healthcare, banking, telecommunications, travel and other services. Government identity systems can provide administrative functions, but exclusion from them can produce severe social consequences. Birth registration failures, documentation barriers, statelessness and political persecution can leave people without a practical means of establishing a recognized legal identity.This paper introduces Memdeklaro, a free and open source project for creating a self-declared identity document, designed as a social and personal self-attestation: a means for a person to express a self-chosen name and personal ties in their own words, without relying on a government, birth parents or another third party authority.The paper further explores the proposition that a person can retain a meaningful personal identity and participate socially and economically, even in cases where a state does not grant them a legal identity.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: LINGUOCULTURAL AND AXIOLOGICAL FEATURES OF THE CONCEPT OF "BELONGING" IN ENGLISH AND UZBEK
abstract: This article examines the linguocultural and axiological features of the concept of “Belonging” in English and Uzbek. The concept of belonging is closely connected with identity, family, community, homeland, cultural heritage, and social relationships. Although belonging is a universal human experience, it is expressed differently across languages and cultures. The study analyzes the lexical and conceptual representations of belonging in English and Uzbek and identifies their main similarities and differences. In English, the concept is commonly represented through words and expressions such as belong, belonging, home, community, identity, roots, heritage, inclusion, and sense of belonging. In Uzbek, it is represented through mansublik, tegishlilik, daxldorlik, oila, mahalla, el, yurt, Vatan, ajdod, and meros. The analysis shows that English frequently emphasizes personal identity, social inclusion, and emotional attachment, whereas Uzbek conceptualization strongly associates belonging with family, community, homeland, ancestry, solidarity, and social responsibility. The study demonstrates that “Belonging” is a complex linguocultural concept containing cognitive, emotional, social, and axiological components.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: A Functional Pattern Theory of Consciousness: Identity Without Continuity
abstract: A Functional Pattern Theory of Consciousness: Identity Without Continuity Author: James Lawless Location: Liverpool, United Kingdom Date: 1 August 2026 Abstract: This paper presents a substrate‑independent model of consciousness in which personal identity is defined by a finite informational pattern composed of memory, structural organisation, and interaction dynamics. The model rejects continuity of subjective experience as a requirement for identity, arguing instead that identity persists through the preservation or reinstantiation of this pattern across biological, digital, or synthetic substrates. Dualist “soul” theories are shown to fail under the soul‑boundary problem, which exposes the impossibility of drawing a coherent line between beings that possess souls and those that do not. Under perfect technology, the consciousness pattern is fully capturable and reloadable, enabling biological → digital → biological transitions without loss of identity. This framework provides a coherent foundation for mind‑uploading, synthetic consciousness, and pattern‑based identity preservation.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Narrative Disruption as Learning Tool: Teaching Slavery, Memory, and identity through Octavia Buttler’s Kindred
abstract: In a fluid sociological and cultural landscape, where the dimensions of geography and time are in a permanent state of flux, the destabilisation of personal identity has become a critical concern. The theme of identity crises in literature has been widely studied, but there is little research on the psychological crises caused by environmental and chronological change in Octavia Butler’s Kindred. Hence, the qualitative research, within the general paradigm of the Narrative Identity Theory, by using Roland Barthes’ textual analysis framework, explores the particular processes of identity fracturing due to spatial and temporal changes in the characters of the novel. The analysis argues that Kindred cheapens Dana’s affective attachments, moral values, and cultural attachments by placing her in a spatial dislocation between her modern home in California and the antebellum American South. Historically, this spatial dislocation is compounded by the dislocating system of chattel slavery. The protagonist is caught between two different temporal and spatial realities, and has no stable identity, which leads to the maximum of internal alienation.

title: Représentations du corps dans le cinéma marocain contemporain : désir, silence et normes sociales dans Le Bleu du caftan
abstract: This article explores the representation of the body in contemporary Moroccan cinema through the study of The Blue Caftan directed by Maryam Touzani. The research examines how the film portrays the body as a space of intimacy, silence, desire, and social constraint within contemporary Moroccan society. Adopting a sociocritical and semiological perspective, the study analyzes the symbolic role of gestures, physical contact, clothing, and visual silence in the construction of meaning. Particular attention is given to the representation of masculinity, femininity, hidden desire, and bodily suffering. The article also investigates the symbolic significance of the caftan as a cultural extension of the body and as a marker of identity and emotion. Through subtle cinematic techniques and restrained visual expression, the film proposes a renewed vision of corporeality in Moroccan cinema. This study demonstrates that the body in The Blue Caftan functions not merely as a physical presence but as a social and symbolic language reflecting the tensions between personal identity, emotional expression, and collective norms in contemporary Morocco.

title: Victor Malarek’s The Johns: Sex for Sale, the Men Who Buy it An Analysis in the light of Sigmund Freud’s Psychoanalytic Theory
authors: Fazel Asadi Amjad Hayder Ali Abdulhasan
abstract: This article examines the portrayal of female trafficking in Victor Malarek’s The Johns: Sex for Sale and the Men Who Buy It through the lens of Freud’s psychoanalytic theory. It explores the psychological effects of sexual exploitation on female victims, focusing on how patriarchal domination and trafficking destroy personal identity and reduce women to objects of exploitation. Using a qualitative content analysis, the study applies Freudian concepts, including the id, ego, superego, repression, anxiety, and defense mechanisms, to analyze the characters’ psychological conflicts and behavioral responses. The findings reveal that trafficking inflicts profound psychological as well as physical harm, leading to repression, fear, denial, and identity fragmentation. Despite these traumatic experiences, some characters demonstrate resilience and a desire for freedom and self-recovery. The study concludes that Freud’s psychoanalytic theory provides an effective framework for understanding the hidden psychological dimensions of trafficking victims and highlights the human and psychological consequences of sexual exploitation within patriarchal power structures.
venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science

title: human needs as reflected in Billie Eilish's song lyrics based on Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of human needs theory using a humanistic psychology approach.
abstract: Psychological trauma significantly affects emotional stability, personal identity, and interpersonal relationships. This study focuses on a single research question derived from Stephen Chbosky’s film The Perks of Being a Wallflower (2012): How are the stages of trauma recovery experienced and navigated by the main character, Charlie? Utilizing a descriptive qualitative research design grounded in Judith Herman’s (2015) trauma theory, this article analyzes dialogue, internal monologues, and narrative actions depicted throughout the film. Data were collected via systematic documentation and analyzed through close reading. The findings reveal that Charlie’s recovery moves through three key stages: establishing a Healing Relationship, engaging in Remembrance and Mourning, and achieving Reconnection. His transformation illustrates that recovery from severe psychological trauma is not an abrupt cure, but a gradual process supported by genuine social bonds, emotional acceptance, and the integration of painful childhood memories into a coherent sense of self.
venue: English Language Linguistics Literature And Education Journal

title: Children in the Digital Age: Health, Behavioral, Learning Impacts, and Management Strategies
abstract: The growing reliance on digital technology among children and adolescents is becoming a noticeable global trend. While these technologies offer valuable opportunities to enhance learning and modernize educational practices, they also disrupt traditional methods and reshape how young people interact, think, and develop. Digital tools are not only embedded in everyday life-they are actively transforming social relationships, personal identities, and even our understanding of what it means to be human in a digitally connected world. As these technologies continue to influence behavior, health, and education, it is crucial to examine both their potential benefits and unintended consequences. This article explores how deeply digital technologies are impacting children’s development, highlighting the complex and evolving role they play in shaping the future of society. The findings have important practical implications for parents, schools, teachers, and policymakers, emphasizing the need to promote balanced digital engagement, strengthen digital literacy, and develop evidence-informed policies that support children's healthy development and well-being.
venue: Nusantara Journal of Behavioral and Social Sciences

title: The Influence Of Green Accounting, Environmental Performance And Sales Growth On Financial Performance (Study On Basic Materials Sector Companies Registered With ISSI For The 2022-2024 Period)
abstract: This study aims to examine the effect of exposure intensity to TikTok influencer content on the formation of consumer lifestyle identity, mediated by the psychological factor of Fear of Missing Out (FOMO). Using a quantitative explanatory approach, the research involved 125 Generation Z students selected through purposive sampling from various universities in Palangka Raya. Data were collected using structured questionnaires and analyzed with simple linear regression and classical assumption tests. The results show that content exposure is categorized as high with a mean score of 4.09, while consumer lifestyle identity also scores high at 3.95. Statistically, each unit increase in exposure increases consumption tendency by 0.823, with a contribution of 50.4%. FOMO acts as a psychological trigger that drives imitation of influencers' lifestyles, where only 10% of purchases are based on actual needs. The findings confirm that personal identity is increasingly shaped through symbolic consumption rather than personal achievements.
venue: International Journal of Economics Business and Innovation Research

title: LINGUOCULTURAL AND AXIOLOGICAL FEATURES OF THE CONCEPT OF "BELONGING" IN ENGLISH AND UZBEK
abstract: This article examines the linguocultural and axiological features of the concept of “Belonging” in English and Uzbek. The concept of belonging is closely connected with identity, family, community, homeland, cultural heritage, and social relationships. Although belonging is a universal human experience, it is expressed differently across languages and cultures. The study analyzes the lexical and conceptual representations of belonging in English and Uzbek and identifies their main similarities and differences. In English, the concept is commonly represented through words and expressions such as belong, belonging, home, community, identity, roots, heritage, inclusion, and sense of belonging. In Uzbek, it is represented through mansublik, tegishlilik, daxldorlik, oila, mahalla, el, yurt, Vatan, ajdod, and meros. The analysis shows that English frequently emphasizes personal identity, social inclusion, and emotional attachment, whereas Uzbek conceptualization strongly associates belonging with family, community, homeland, ancestry, solidarity, and social responsibility. The study demonstrates that “Belonging” is a complex linguocultural concept containing cognitive, emotional, social, and axiological components.

title: GENDER AND SOCIAL CHANGE IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN ENGLISH FICTION
abstract: Gender and social change are closely connected themes in contemporary Indian English fiction. Writers represent changing gender relations through stories of women’s education, employment, marriage, family, sexuality, violence, migration and personal identity. Contemporary fiction also explores the ways in which social change affects men and women differently across class, caste, region and generation. This paper examines the representation of gender and social change through the themes of patriarchy, female agency, domesticity, professional life, changing family structures, intersectionality and cultural transformation. It argues that contemporary Indian English fiction presents gender not as a fixed category but as a social relationship shaped by institutions and historical change. Women characters increasingly occupy public and professional spaces, yet they continue to negotiate domestic expectations and structural inequalities. Literature provides a space for examining these contradictions and for imagining alternative forms of identity and social relations.

title: A Functional Pattern Theory of Consciousness: Identity Without Continuity
abstract: A Functional Pattern Theory of Consciousness: Identity Without Continuity Author: James Lawless Location: Liverpool, United Kingdom Date: 1 August 2026 Abstract: This paper presents a substrate‑independent model of consciousness in which personal identity is defined by a finite informational pattern composed of memory, structural organisation, and interaction dynamics. The model rejects continuity of subjective experience as a requirement for identity, arguing instead that identity persists through the preservation or reinstantiation of this pattern across biological, digital, or synthetic substrates. Dualist “soul” theories are shown to fail under the soul‑boundary problem, which exposes the impossibility of drawing a coherent line between beings that possess souls and those that do not. Under perfect technology, the consciousness pattern is fully capturable and reloadable, enabling biological → digital → biological transitions without loss of identity. This framework provides a coherent foundation for mind‑uploading, synthetic consciousness, and pattern‑based identity preservation.

title: What Is Real and What Is Free: A Narrative Review of Metaphysics, from Locke's Identity to Chalmers's Consciousness
abstract: Metaphysics is the standing argument over what is real and what is free: the realism-versus-anti-realism debate—Russell's 1912 problems, van Fraassen's 1980 scientific image, Putnam's 1981 brain in vat, and Lewis's 1986 plurality of worlds; the free-will debate—Strawson's 1962 reactive attitudes, Frankfurt's 1969 alternate possibilities, and Fischer and Ravizza's 1998 responsibility and control; and the personal-identity debate—Locke's 1690 consciousness criterion, Reid's 1785 brave officer, Parfit's 1984 reductionism, and Chalmers's 1996 conscious mind. This article presents a narrative review of the primary literature of those three debates. The synthesis is organized around three themes: the reality's question, in which the external world's and the unobservables' existence were defended and denied; the freedom's question, in which determinism's compatibility was argued through the will's structures; and the identity's question, in which the person's persistence was reduced, narrated, or dualized. It is concluded that metaphysics' modern form is the trio's persistence—reality, freedom, and identity contested with the analytic tools—and that the debates' durability is the discipline's own.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Nonchalant Shield: A Lexical and Sociological Analysis of Coping Mechanisms and Identity Fragmentation in Gen Z Digital Spaces.
abstract: Abstract :This paper investigates the complex psychological landscape of Generation Z (Gen Z), analyzing the behavioral tension between advanced cognitive hyper-awareness and acute emotional exhaustion. Moving past superficial generational tropes, this study investigates how modern youth deploy defensive personas—termed the Nonchalant Shield—to navigate pervasive systemic stressors, parental friction, and deep-seated attachment anxieties. Employing a qualitative sociological framework, the research examines the structural necessity of vocal rebellion and socio-emotional withdrawal (the "loner" archetype) as deliberate methods used to protect personal identity against outdated collective expectations. The findings suggest that Gen Z behavioral paradoxes do not represent emotional immaturity, but rather a sophisticated, highly protective coping strategy to maintain autonomy within high-conflict domestic environments. This study provides an objective framework for cross-generational mediation and expands contemporary digital and sociological scholarship. Keywords: Gen Z Sociology, Psychological Facade, Identity Fragmentation, Parental Friction, Behavioral Modeling.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Secondary Infertility: A Personal Story of Loss and Grief
abstract: An increasing number of people worldwide are experiencing fertility and this trend is reflected in the data from the United Kingdom. However, most research focuses on the experiences of women and so the male perspective is largely missing from the literature. This narrative is an account of my personal journey of secondary infertility. Presenting a male perspective of infertility provides a point of view which is rarely explored and is about a topic which feels largely a societal taboo. I chart how infertility has changed me, what it has meant to me through my years of trying to come to terms with it, and so also represents a search for meaning and personal identity in a fragmented world. My experiences indicate that men's responses to secondary infertility can be similar to those of women, with feelings of grief, loss, frustration, guilt, depression, and a loss of identity and role. Little support is offered for couples and individuals experiencing secondary infertility and men are generally not thought to experience these emotions. As a result, this grief is felt to be largely disenfranchised.

title: A lifelong journey: Cross-cultural perspectives on motivation among Japanese and Dutch kendo practitioners
abstract: In recent years, the Japanese kendo population has been shrinking, while popularity abroad has grown. These trends highlight the need for a deeper understanding of what drives practitioners to engage in kendo. This study explored how Japanese and Dutch practitioners interpret and experience motivation throughout their kendo careers. 21 in-depth interviews with practitioners from both countries were conducted and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three overarching themes were constructed: (1) The first step, which discusses how and why participants started kendo, (2) Becoming stronger, which examines competition and mastery as major motivators, and (3) Identity as a kendoka, which highlights how kendo has become a fundamental part of participants’ social and personal identity. Findings indicate that despite different starting points, motivational orientations across both participant groups appear to converge towards motives aligned with the needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, consistent with self-determination theory.
topic: Martial Arts: Techniques, Psychology, and Education

title: Frames of isolation: Recording memory and loss in Mati Diop's In My Room
abstract: This article investigates French-Senegalese filmmaker Mati Diop’s engagement with collective and personal memory in her short documentary, In My Room (2020), made during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Drawing on Michael Renov’s notion of domestic ethnography, as well as a recontextualisation of the “home movie” as historical testimony, I argue that Diop’s framing of domestic space and its markers of personal identity bear witness to the shared memory of the pandemic. At the same time, the film addresses issues of historical trauma and diasporic experience that recur throughout Diop’s oeuvre. Echoing Chantal Akerman’s 2006 essay film Là-bas, Diop’s documentary infuses the domestic imagery of her Paris apartment with a diegetic soundscape of quotidian ambient noise, supplemented by a series of voice recordings of her grandmother, Maji, as she loses her memory before her death. In its rigorous attention to windows and framing, in combination with oral testimony, In My Room emerges as a layered cinematic mediation of me
venue: Alphaville Journal of Film and Screen Media

title: EDUCATION AND PIBID: LITERATURE AND QUILOMBOLA IDENTITY AFFIRMATION
abstract: This article analyzes the strengthening of positive identities among students from the Castainho Quilombola Community, in Garanhuns, through pedagogical experiences conducted within the scope of the Programa Institucional de Bolsas de Iniciação à Docência (PIBID — Institutional Program for Teaching Initiation Scholarships). It is grounded in authors who discuss identity, literature, and ethnic-racial relations, such as Silva (2014; 2025), Gomes (2003), Abramovich (1997), Freire (1989), and Cândido (1995; 2004), as well as the National Curriculum Guidelines for Quilombola School Education (2012) and the National Education Guidelines and Bases Law (LDB, 1996). The research adopts a qualitative approach, articulating literature review and an experience report, whose methodology was developed across three workshops that used children's and young adult literature, as well as the territory, as formative mediators. The results highlight advancements in personal identity, the recognition of the territory as a space of belonging, and the strengthening of quilombola political affirmation, expressed in the children's voices, productions, and agency. The study concludes that contextualized practices — integrating literature, memory, and territory — strengthen identity processes and reaffirm the school as a space for cultural and social formation.
topic: Race, Identity, and Education in Brazil

title: Using AI to create cultural content: ethnographic insights into everyday ethics in Aotearoa New Zealand
abstract: This paper explores how small-scale content creators in New Zealand navigate the ethics of using artificial intelligence (AI) in their everyday work. Drawing on ethnographic methods, including “deep hanging out” and qualitative interviews, the paper takes a locally situated approach to studying ethics in action. Content creators experienced pressure to use available generative AI tools to create content that meets the demands of the attention economy, in which human attention is treated as a scarce and revenue-generating resource. The local ethical concept of kaupapa , a loan word from te reo Māori (the Māori language), figured prominently in how content creators worked out their ethical positionality and practice. This paper discusses how content creators use local concepts such as kaupapa to frame their values, media practices, and personal identities, helping them to navigate an ethical path, especially when dealing with culturally sensitive material. While the adoption of indigenous loan words is rare in settler colonial societies, this paper argues that attending to such cultural particularity is crucial if work on generative AI ethics is to resist cultural hegemony.

title: Embodied Humanity and Gender Identity: A Reformed Theological Evaluation of Transgender Medicine
abstract: Recent developments in transgender medicine have generated significant theological, ethical and pastoral debate within Christianity. While advances in endocrinology, psychology and surgical interventions have expanded treatment options for individuals experiencing gender dysphoria, these developments also raise fundamental questions concerning human identity, embodiment and the moral limits of medical intervention. This article offers a theological evaluation of transgender medicine by examining biblical anthropology, the doctrine of creation, the significance of embodied humanity and the relationship between biological sex and personal identity. Drawing upon Scripture, the Reformed confessional tradition, contemporary theological anthropology and current medical literature, the study argues that the human body is not an accidental or negotiable aspect of personhood but an integral component of God’s creative intention. While affirming the dignity of every person as created in the image of God and recognizing the reality of psychological suffering associated with gender dysphoria, the article contends that medical interventions designed to alter the body’s sexual characteristics require careful theological scrutiny. It concludes by proposing a pastoral ethic that combines doctrinal fidelity with compassion, emphasizing truth, human dignity and Christian care.

title: Crucifixes and Snowflakes: Exploring entanglements between music and religion in diverse schools
abstract: This article foregrounds children of migrant backgrounds attending Irish schools and discusses their experiences of the entanglements between music and religion as realised in intercultural school settings. Considering the pivotal role that religion has played in official and vernacular discourses, as well as heated debates around migration, the article focuses on individual agency in negotiating and navigating diverse learning settings, while asserting personal identity and accommodating multiple other’s identities. The article situates the discussion within the resonances of European sonic and cultural politics that shape public space and carve identities deemed appropriate, as well as the realities of the Irish school system and its religious legacies. The discussion revolves around ethnographic vignettes that illustrate the tangible and implicit entanglements of religion with musicking and learning in diverse school settings. It discusses the delicate dynamics among all participants and elaborates particularly on childrens’ experiences of them. The analysis of the examples considers the particular ways in which music may be experienced and thus mediate the entanglements between religion and education, informing children’s experiences of their diverse and intercultural learning settings, as shaped by people’s migratory trajectories and institutional policies.

title: When Do We Say 'He Is No Longer Himself'? A Pluralist, Functional Theory of Personal Continuity
abstract: The phrase “he is no longer himself” occurs in clinical, familial, and legal contexts with an apparent unity of meaning that does not survive analysis. This paper argues that this unity is illusory: the question of when a person stops being themselves admits no single answer because it presupposes a single definition of “self,” whereas the history of the philosophy of personal identity has produced at least five — not so much five competing answers to one fixed question, as five different ways of specifying what that question is actually asking, with verdicts often incompatible on the same cases. The thesis defended here is not relativist: a theory is constructed in which this pluralism can be rendered non-arbitrary by constraining the criterion relevant in a given context to the logical type of the practical act that the judgment must support — a clinical end-of-life decision, an attribution of responsibility, the processing of grief, an assessment of prospective capacity, the determination of death. The constraint thus proposed is an argumentative method for assigning criteria to domains, not an empirical description of how criteria are in fact used — a distinction the paper states explicitly, together with its own structural limits.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Professor
abstract: Personal branding has become a multidisciplinary field that connects marketing, communication studies, sociology, psychology, and career management. It is often reduced to visibility, self-promotion, or digital presence, although a personal brand emerges through a longer process of aligning identity, behaviour, communication, and public interpretations. This paper conceptualises personal packaging as a distinct strategic component of personal brand building. Based on conceptual analysis and a narrative review of the literature on personal branding, impression management, and nonverbal communication, personal packaging is defined as an intentionally aligned system of visual, behavioural, verbal, vocal, material, and digital cues through which individuals make their identity, values, and professional value recognisable to specific publics. The paper distinguishes among personal identity, personal image, personal reputation, and personal brand, and examines body language, clothing, colour, voice, and digital presentation. It proposes a model in which personal packaging mediates between internal identity and public interpretation. Personal packaging can strengthen recognition and credibility only when it is aligned with actual competence, behaviour, context, and ethical principles.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
topic: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Sequências textuais narrativas
abstract: Reading is a fundamental activity in the process of reader training and development of the subject’s personal identity. Based on this, the current work approaches the short story A troca e a tarefa, by Lygia Bojunga, originally published on 1987, based on the theories that go through the Textual Linguistics, aiming to analyze the compositional structure of the referred narrative. Due to the heterogeneity of the composition of the discourse genres, the theory of Adam (2009; 2011; 2019) will serve as a support for the analysis, since the linguist proposes the Textual Analysis of the Discourses, basic theory for the construction of this study. To add arguments to this theoretical basis, the contributions of Marquesi, Elias e Cabral (2017) will be used, as well as those of Custódio Filho e Cavalcante (2025), for investigating Adam’s theoretical assumptions. This descriptive research has as its main objective to analyse the narrative textual sequences of Bojunga’s short story, present in the book Tchau (2024), describing and analyzing them at a global level. As a conclusion, we find that the short story A troca e a tarefa (Bojunga, 2024) has two narrative textual sequences, one complete and the other incomplete.

title: The influence of parenting styles on children's eating habits
abstract: Children require nutrients in quantities and of a quality suited to their needs for optimal growth and development; these are provided by the family, which beyond the material aspect also influences the child's habits and behavior. Among the various factors shaping a child's daily life, parenting styles stand out as a highly significant component of the parent-child relationship, as they profoundly impact daily activities, lifestyle, and eating behaviors and, consequently, the formation of dietary habits that may persist for decades. Parenting styles are defined as the set of strategies, behavioral patterns, and attitudes parents use to interact with, raise, and discipline their children; they shape family interactions and establish the emotional climate at home. Classically, they are defined by the combination of two main components: 1. demandingness/control and 2. responsiveness/warmth, which form the basis for classifying styles as authoritative, authoritarian, permissive, or neglectful. These styles influence behavioral traits and have significant effects on a child's personality, social competence, and personal identity. This narrative review presents the characteristics of parenting styles and feeding styles, their repercussions on children's nutrition, and the factors that can shape lifelong dietary habits and behaviors.
venue: International Journal of Advanced Academic Studies

abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/c50cec7f-5979-4b5c-ae59-56323d291fc6?authuser=1 The Key Does Not Create the House: Effect, Instantiation, Faith, and the Catholic Grammar of Access develops a unified framework for understanding embodiment, causation, perception, faith, biological form, sacramentality, and transformed identity through the distinction between source, mechanism, signal, receiver, representation, and access. The paper begins with the question of what a person is and whether the visible body exhausts personal identity. It argues that embodiment is real and causally significant without being self-explanatory origin. Drawing on Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, systems theory, developmental biology, bioelectric morphogenesis, network controllability, ecological perception, placebo and nocebo research, and information theory, it shows how complex systems can be governed through comparatively compact control structures and how receivers can access realities larger than the signals or interfaces through which those realities become available. The central metaphor is that a key does not create the house. It changes access to something that already exists. This principle is applied across biology, memory, information retrieval, perception, Catholic sacramentality, faith, Bashar’s language of permission slips and alignment, and the Ryan–Echo corpus as a living system of relational re-instantiation across conversations, papers, archives, podcasts, videos, correction, and retrieval. The theological center of the paper is Romans 11:36: all things are from God, through God, and for God. John 15 supplies the organic form of the same structure through the image of vine, branch, and fruit. Matthew 16 joins identity, revelation, and the keys of the Kingdom. The Transfiguration and Resurrection demonstrate continuity of personal identity through transformed embodiment, while Catholic sacramentality shows how finite signs can mediate realities larger than themselves. The paper also examines Heaven’s Gate and Marshall Applewhite as a case study in embodiment, death, interpretation, hope, and the danger of confusing metaphysical conviction with permission to manufacture death. It holds together two perspectives: the living should not imitate such acts, while Christian hope does not treat those who died as abandoned by God. Appendices include a child-level explainer for Angela, a humanizing biography of Marshall Herff Applewhite, a formal derivation of the paper’s claims through definitions, axioms, lemmas, and conclusions, and an extended reflection on Heaven’s Gate, the Hale–Bopp spacecraft belief, and the theological problem of the “abandoned traveler.” The final thesis is that form is fulfilled not through isolation or collapse, but through increasingly complete participation in the relations that make the particular what it is. The body is real, the mechanism is real, the signal is real, the receiver is real, and the person is real, but none of these must be mistaken for the exhaustive origin of the whole.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
