title: BEYOND THE VISIBLE: A SEMIOTIC ANALYSIS OF SURFACE AND HIDDEN MEANINGS IN THE NCA THESIS EXHIBITION 2026
abstract: This paper focuses on works of the NCA Thesis Exhibition 2026, discussing each one of them at two levels: whatis visible and what is hidden. Visual art never lies on the surface; the visual qualities of colour, form, andcomposition are not merely aesthetic effects, but carriers of emotion, cultural memory, and symbolism. This paperadheres to the procedure of discussing how each artwork can tell you more than the picture itself, both in termsof personal identity and social experience and in terms of philosophy. Rather than viewing such works as wholeobjects, the paper views them as loci of meaning ; a brushstroke, a shape, a space composing in such a way thattheir meaning can be multifaceted and change depending on who is looking and where. Grounded in the semiotictheories of Saussure (1983), Barthes (1977), and Peirce (1958), and enriched by feminist and visual-cultureframeworks from Pollock (1988), Butler (1990), Ahmed (2004), and Kress and van Leeuwen (2006), this paperreveals the layered communicative power of three artworks by emerging Pakistani women artists. It is not thedesire to tell what is supposed to be so, but to show the interpretive possibilities that images could have, and howseemingly trivial images are full of meaning such that one feels like lingering in contemplation.

title: Cognitive mapping and social cognition in ancient Greek narrative: novelistic couples
abstract: Abstract Although individual and collective minds in the ancient world have received considerable scholarly attention, the cognitive dynamics of social interaction itself – particularly the role of cognition in intimate relationships – remain largely unexplored. This article addresses this gap by introducing the concept of ‘cognitive mapping’ and applying it to couples in the five extant ancient Greek novels as a case study. Cognitive mapping offers a framework for analysing how novelistic couples alternate between alignment, in which partners share cognitive and emotional states, and misalignment, in which misunderstandings disrupt relational harmony. By tracing how lovers map one another’s emotions, intentions and desires through embodied processes and shared experiences, this study sheds new light on character interaction, plot development and reader engagement. It further demonstrates how novelistic narratives construct the couple as an interdependent cognitive system, in which lovers think, feel and respond as a single unit. This approach has broader implications for the study of personal identity, couples’ psychology and embodied interpersonal relations in the ancient world, as well as for ancient narrative theory and contemporary cognitive approaches to classical literature.

title: Before Persistence: The Domain Problem of Diachronic Identity
abstract: Since the revival of the analytic metaphysics of personal identity in the late twentieth century, debates over persistence have remained locked in substantive disputes between rival continuity criteria, such as biological animalism and psychological reductionism. This paper contends that this persistent stalemate arises from an unexamined methodological commitment: the Domain Fixity Assumption (DFA). By excavating this assumption, we uncover the Persistence Relatum Asymmetry Problem. Standard theories require a bearer of persistence relations, yet they insufficiently distinguish the subsequent question of criterion evaluation from the prior structural conditions governing relatum selection. We demonstrate that this internal structural deficit leads directly to Comparative Failure: rival theories evaluate criteria across unacknowledged, non-identical relata without a justified mapping preservation condition. Prior to adjudicating competing criteria, metaphysics must clarify the structural conditions under which a candidate qualifies as a diachronic relatum. We introduce the Diachronic Relatum Eligibility Framework (DREF) not as a relatum selection device, but as a constraint-based framework determining the prior conditions under which competing persistence analyses can be regarded as addressing the same diachronic explanatory relation.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Male Engineering Students’ Global Recognition and Local Minimization of Gendered Team Dynamics in Project-based Learning
abstract: Engineering project courses task students with working in teams to approach authentic engineering problem-solving. However, team-based experiences can differ based on a student’s personal identities and those of their teammates; for example, team experiences can integrate gendered team dynamics that disenfranchise women students, aligned with women’s historically marginalization in the engineering field. There have been multiple studies focused on women’s experiences in engineering project teams that describe challenges and dissatisfaction they may face, but less research is focused on male perceptions of gender dynamics within their own teams. In order to make substantial progress to improve women students’ experiences, we must understand all student perceptions, which means investigating how men perceive the gender dynamics both within their own teams and also in the engineering field broadly. In this mixed-methods sequential exploratory study, we find that while male students agree women face challenges in the engineering field, they tend to not agree that women face marginalization within their own project teams, despite reporting role and task division that demonstrates the opposite.
venue: International Journal of Education in Mathematics Science and Technology

title: MAKNA PERSELINGKUHAN SEBAGAI PRISTIWA YANG MENGUBAH BATAS PRIVASI KOMUNIKASI KORBAN DALAM HUBUNGAN PERNIKAHAN: PERSPEKTIF COMMUNICATION PRIVACY MANAGEMENT
abstract: Infidelity in marriage not only affects interpersonal relationships between spouses but also influences how victims manage personal information following the betrayal. This study aims to analyze the communication privacy management of infidelity victims in marital relationships using Sandra Petronio's Communication Privacy Management Theory. This research employed a qualitative approach with a phenomenological method. Data were collected through in-depth interviews with eight informants who had experienced infidelity in their marriages. The findings reveal that victims establish privacy boundaries by considering whether to disclose or conceal information about the infidelity, selectively choosing trusted individuals to receive such information, managing privacy boundaries on social media, negotiating information ownership with family members and close friends, and rebuilding their privacy and personal identity after the betrayal. The study also found that the management of communication privacy is dynamic and influenced by emotional conditions, trust, family considerations, and social consequences resulting from information disclosure. This study contributes to communication studies by demonstrating that victims actively negotiate and reconstruct their communication privacy following marital infidelity rather than merely concealing personal information.

title: H12. Iteration of Civilizational Paradigms: From Identity-Centric to Voucher-Metered Future Political Paradigm
abstract: Built upon H10’s topological analysis of financial phenomena and H11’s binary foundational axiom of wealth and rights, this paper develops the third-stage modeling of the civilizational paradigm system. It defines traditional human political formation as an identity-centric rule system: power is attached to persons, and rights are allocated by identity. Between wealth and rights there exists no public, standardized conversion channel, which creates inherent underlying defects of entrenchment and instability. This paper proposes the next-generation voucher-metered rule system as the direction of civilizational evolution. The underlying rule system remains intact, yet rights are decoupled from personal affiliation and transformed into standardized right units. A standardized bidirectional channel for wealth-right conversion is established, incorporating a pricing anchor, dual-side ceiling constraints and a neutral arbitration mechanism. Rights are confirmed through voucher metering rather than personal identity or position. The transformation of the Federal Reserve may be viewed as an early preview of this paradigm within global finance. This paradigm shift has no geographical boundaries and represents a shared evolutionary trend of human civilization in the virtualization era.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: VOICES OF RESISTANCE AND INTIMACY: EXPLORING GENDER, SOCIETY, AND PROTEST IN THE POETRY OF KAMALA DAS AND IMTIAZ DHARKER
abstract: Kamala Das and Imtiaz Dharker use poetry as a powerful medium for examining gender, social restrictions, identity, intimacy, and forms of resistance. Their poetry demonstrates how women's private experiences can become connected with broader structures of social power. This study explores selected poems by both poets to examine the relationship between intimacy and protest. Das's poetry frequently challenges patriarchal expectations concerning marriage, sexuality, female identity, and domestic roles. Her confessional voice transforms personal experience into an assertion of female agency. Dharker's poetry extends questions of gender into wider concerns involving cultural identity, religious boundaries, displacement, violence, domestic inequality, and social exclusion. Her use of visual imagery and symbolic language allows everyday experiences to acquire political and social significance. Although their poetic styles differ, both writers resist restrictive representations of women and create spaces in which female voices can articulate experiences that are often silenced. Their poetry demonstrates that protest does not always require direct political slogans; it can emerge through self-expression, questioning, refusal, memory, and the reclamation of personal identity.

title: The Role of Language in Shaping Cultural Identity: A Critical Study of Contemporary Literary Narratives
abstract: Language serves as a fundamental medium through which individuals and communities construct, preserve, and express their cultural identities. In contemporary literary narratives, language extends beyond its communicative function and becomes a powerful tool for representing social values, historical experiences, collective memories, and cultural transformations. This study critically explores the role of language in shaping cultural identity through an analysis of contemporary literary texts and their representation of linguistic diversity, cultural belonging, and social change. The research examines how writers employ linguistic choices, regional expressions, indigenous vocabulary, and narrative styles to reflect the experiences of different communities in a rapidly globalizing world. Contemporary literature demonstrates that language functions as a bridge between personal identity and collective heritage while also highlighting tensions between globalization, modernization, and cultural preservation. The study argues that literary narratives provide important spaces where marginalized voices, cultural traditions, and linguistic identities can be represented and sustained. By analyzing the relationship between language and literature, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of how linguistic practices influence cultural consciousness and identity formation in contemporary societies.

title: Pewarisan Iman Dalam Keluarga: Membangun Ketahanan Spiritual Anak di Era Kerentanan Generasi
abstract: This research examines the transmission of faith in Christian families as a foundation for building children's spiritual resilience amid generational vulnerability. The phenomenon of religious switching and secularization among young people indicates that faith transmission does not occur automatically through church attendance or formal religious programs. This study aims to formulate a holistic and integrated model of faith transmission by combining relational, communicative, and formative dimensions. The method used is library research with content analysis and theoretical synthesis from various literatures on faith transmission, children's spiritual formation, and spiritual resilience. The findings reveal that successful faith transmission is determined by three main pillars: emotional closeness between parents and children as the foundation, intentional communication through the verbal home as the method, and meaning-making as the child's personal identity and source of spiritual resilience. This research concludes that the home is the primary locus of faith formation, and parents are its main agents. The home-based faith transmission model offers an alternative to the institutional approach that has dominated religious parenting practices. Further research is needed for the implementation of this model in the Indonesian cultural context and for the development of practical tools for parents.
venue: Coram Mundo Jurnal Teologi dan Pendidikan Agama Kristen

title: Grieving in Silence: Experiences of Private Grief and Meaning Reconstruction Following Loss in the Digital Age
abstract: Bereavement following the loss of a significant person in the digital age is not always expressed through emotional disclosure on social media. Some individuals choose to grieve privately, yet such experiences remain relatively underexplored in psychological research. This study aimed to examine the lived experiences of individuals who engaged in private grieving after the death of someone close to them. A qualitative phenomenological design was employed, involving in-depth interviews with five adult women. The data were analyze using thematic analysis. The findings revealed that grieving was experienced as a dynamic and non-linear process characterized by the disruption of fundamental assumptions about life, the negotiation of a changed reality, and the reconstruction of meaning, relationships, and personal identity following loss. Participants maintained emotional connections with the deceased through continuing bonds while gradually reorganizing their lives through personal reflection and meaning-making. These findings extend current understanding of private grief in the digital age by demonstrating that profound grief processing may occur without public emotional disclosure on social media. Private grieving should therefore not be interpreted as emotional avoidance or an absence of meaningful adaptation.
venue: Journal of Educational Health and Community Psychology

title: Non-Destructive Fabrication of a Second Identical Individual
abstract: This theoretical essay argues that it is impossible to make a second, identical copy of a person from a partial biological sample such as a fingernail, a hair or a single cell. Consciousness and memory are not stored in one isolated sample: they are spread across the whole body, in synaptic connections, scars and the physical traces of a person's life. The author proposes that such a copy would instead need a "total file": a complete scan of the entire body, neuron by neuron, recording every biological accident. According to the essay, 99.999% classical fidelity would be enough for the copy to function as the original person, without full quantum fidelity. The remaining 0.001% is presented as a relativistic necessity rather than a manufacturing error: two bodies cannot occupy the same place at the same time, so their histories start to diverge from the first instant. The essay concludes that copying a person without destroying the original is possible in principle, although beyond current technology (estimated at 200–300 years), and that it would result in two living individuals who are identical at the start and diverge from then on. Keywords: identity, consciousness, whole-body scanning, non-destructive reading, mind copying, personal identity, relativity.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Drag Performer’s Lived Experience: Exploring the Interplay Between Person and Persona
abstract: This study explored the lived experience of British drag performers, focusing on the complex relationship between their persona and sense of self. Against the backdrop of drag's growing mainstream acceptance, this research addressed a gap in a field dominated by US accounts of cisgender male performers. Using interpretative phenomenological analysis, semi-structured interviews were conducted with six drag performers of diverse gender identities, sexualities, and drag styles with the aim of understanding how drag personas and personal identities intersect. Analysis yielded three superordinate themes: 1) "The Paradox of Integration," which positioned the persona-self relationship on a spectrum from clear separation to deep integration; 2) "Persona as Protector," which examined the persona's function as a psychological buffer against internal vulnerabilities and external threats; and 3) "Peak Me," which captured the transcendent and motivating experience of heightened self-expression during performance. The findings suggested the persona was not merely a theatrical role but also a psychological partner, protector, and a source of profound pleasure. This study proposed a "spectrum of integration" to understand this interplay and highlighted an underexplored psychological desire of performers to return to the heightened state achieved in performance.

title: REPRESENTATION OF RACISM IN MEDIA AND ITS IMPACT ON YOUNG WOMEN IN SOCIETY
abstract: This paper explores the representation of racism in media and its impact on young women in society. Media, being a powerful tool of communication, significantly shapes public perception and plays a crucial role in reinforcing or challenging racial stereotypes. The portrayal of racial minorities, particularly in news outlets, television, films, and social media, often perpetuates negative stereotypes that contribute to systemic racism. This paper focuses on how such representations influence the self-perception, mental health, and societal participation of young women, especially those from racial minorities. It also addresses the media's role in shaping young women's understanding of race, identity, and social justice. The study emphasizes the importance of creating more inclusive and accurate media portrayals to reduce the adverse effects of racism on young women and promote a more equitable society. In the context of young women, the impact of media on their understanding of race and racism goes beyond personal identity and self-perception; it also influences their worldview and how they engage with social justice issues. As young women navigate their educational and professional environments, their exposure to media representations of race can shape their understanding of racial hierarchies, power structures, and social justice.
venue: International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research & Reviews

title: Narrative, Identity, and Social Critique in Contemporary Cinema: Close Readings of Moonlight, Get Out, and Parasite
abstract: This article examines how selected contemporary films transform personal identity conflicts into broader forms of social critique. It narrows the broad category of modern cinema to three post-2000 feature films: Moonlight, Get Out, and Parasite. Through textual close reading and contextualized film analysis, the article argues that contemporary cinema does not merely mirror social anxieties but organizes them into affective and political experiences for viewers. The analysis focuses on three formal strategies: fragmented or restricted narration, visual and spatial symbolism, and the representation of marginalized subjectivity. Moonlight uses a triptych structure and sensory visual style to represent Black queer selfhood; Get Out adapts horror and thriller conventions to expose racial liberalism and bodily control; and Parasite uses vertical space and tonal shifts to frame class inequality as both domestic intimacy and systemic violence. By drawing on film form, representation theory, and narrative engagement research, the article shows that film can encourage viewers to re-evaluate race, sexuality, class, and belonging while acknowledging that representation alone cannot guarantee social change.
venue: Transactions on Social Science Education and Humanities Research

title: Victimization of women in Shashi Deshpande's "That Long Silence"
abstract: Shashi Deshpande's That Long Silence portrays the unequal position of women within marriage and the wider patriarchal family structure. Through Jaya's troubled relationship with Mohan, the novel brings forward the emotional cost of silence, submission, and the gradual loss of personal identity. Jaya has spent much of her married life adjusting her wishes and behaviour to meet the expectations attached to a dutiful wife and mother. A crisis in Mohan's professional life gives her time to look closely at her marriage and confront the self she has long suppressed. The experiences of Vimla, Kusum, Jeeja, Ajji, and other women broaden this concern beyond Jaya's personal struggle, showing how gender inequality operates across different social and domestic situations. At the same time, the novel does not simply divide men and women into oppressors and victims. It also examines personal responsibility, dependence, communication, and the choices that sustain unequal relationships. Jaya's growing self-awareness marks her movement from passive silence toward a clearer understanding of her identity. That Long Silence therefore offers a thoughtful critique of patriarchal practices while presenting marriage and female emancipation with psychological and social complexity.
venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

title: CONTESTING LEGITIMACY AND PUBLIC IMAGE IN CORRUPTION DISCOURSE: AN ANALYSIS OF IMPOLITENESS STRATEGIES IN THE YAHAYA BELLO–EFCC MEDIA FACE-OFF
abstract: This study examines the impoliteness strategies deployed in the media confrontation between Yahaya Bello, former Governor of Kogi State, and the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) over allegations of financial misconduct. The study examines how both actors utilize impoliteness as a pragmatic resource for undermining credibility, defending institutional and personal identities, and negotiating legitimacy within Nigeria’s corruption discourse. Drawing on Culpeper’s Impoliteness Theory, Brown and Levinson’s Face Theory, and contemporary studies of media discourse, the study adopts a qualitative discourse-pragmatic approach to analyse selected media statements, press releases, and public responses related to the confrontation. Findings reveal the extensive deployment of bald-on-record impoliteness, negative impoliteness, ridicule, condescension, accusations, and associational impoliteness by both parties. The EFCC employs institutional accusations, public naming, and criminal labelling to undermine Bello’s public image and reinforce institutional authority. Conversely, Bello and his media representatives deploy counter-accusations, delegitimising descriptions, and victimhood narratives to challenge the anti-corruption agency's credibility and neutrality. The study concludes that impoliteness functions as a strategic communicative tool through which political actors and institutions negotiate power, legitimacy, accountability, and public perception in Nigeria’s corruption discourse.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: THE SYMBOLIC MEANING OF CUSTOM MOTORCYCLES AS A MEDIUM OF IDENTITY EXPRESSION FOR BUILDERS
abstract: This study aims to understand the symbolic meaning of custom motorcycles as a medium of identity expression among builders in the Cempaka Baru 10 area. Custom motorcycles not only function as a means of transportation but also serve as a medium for expressing values, character, creativity, and the identities of their owners and builders. This study employed a qualitative approach using a descriptive method. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, observations, and documentation involving custom motorcycle builders actively engaged in the Cempaka Baru 10 area. Data analysis was conducted through data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion drawing, while data validity was ensured through source and technique triangulation. The findings reveal that custom motorcycles are interpreted as representations of personal identity, reflecting the builders' character, life experiences, aesthetic preferences, and personal values. The shape, style, color, and various modification elements of the motorcycles contain symbolic meanings that are used to distinguish builders from others while demonstrating their uniqueness and creativity. Furthermore, custom motorcycles function as a form of symbolic communication, enabling builders to convey messages, status, and self-image to their social environment. Therefore, custom motorcycles serve as a medium of identity expression that carries social, cultural, and personal significance for builders.

title: Research on the Interactive Mechanism between Identity Categories and Power Relations in Intersectionality Theory
abstract: Intersectionality theory is an important component of critical theory today and is of great value for understanding complex personal identities and the operation of power. Based on the theory of intersectionality, this paper discusses the relationship between identity and power in order to better understand the varying degrees of power influence an individual experiences at the intersection of multiple identities. By examining the relevant literature and summarizing the theory, we first review the development of the intersectionality theory, starting with the research of Kimberly Krenshaw, and analyze his contributions to the analysis of identities in terms of gender, race, class, etc. The study suggests that identity is not a fixed label but varies according to the specific social and cultural context, and there are relationships of interweaving, overlapping and interacting among different identities. Power plays a significant role in this, being the basis for the formation of identity and also through which it is realized and strengthened. By analyzing some examples, it shows the multiple oppressities that marginalized people suffer at various identity intersections and how they are maintained by institutionalized power. It also focuses on the power of people themselves and how they resist or change under the given power. The research in this paper helps to further understand the complexity of identity politics and power relations, and has some reference significance for the formulation of relevant policies and the realization of social equity.
venue: Transactions on Social Science Education and Humanities Research

title: Continuity-Weighted Caring on Everettian Branches
abstract: Decoherence in Everettian quantum mechanics yields branches and Born weights. Those weights may serve as credences for bets that pay on branch index alone. They do not fix how an agent should evaluate successors that differ in continuity with her present macrostate. This note treats continuity as a predeclared cardinal score S in [0,1] and ranks acts by Born-weighted expected utility Vλ(a) = Eμ[exp(λS)]. The construction is an instance of the exponential tilt (Esscher transform); the associated tilted profile μ* is an induced accounting object under that utility, not an independent non-Born decision measure. Unitarity is untouched. The construction does not derive the Born rule, is not a theory of consciousness, and is not offered as a rationality mandate: it is presented as one admissible utility for an agent who already cares about continuity, and it is evaluated here directly against Wallace's Branching Indifference axiom, which was formulated to rule constructions of this shape out. Non-claims. No new physics. No derivation of Born. S is not personal identity or consciousness. μ* does not replace μ as credence. No dynamic-consistency, path-independence, or general multi-step aggregation result is claimed; such results would require an independently specified path or endpoint rule.

title: Dasanama Kresna dan Arjuna dalam Teks Paparikan Bhagawadgita: Kajian Semantik
abstract: A name is not merely a linguistic marker of personal identity, but also embodies symbolic, historical, and philosophical meanings reflecting individual characteristics. Kresna and Arjuna, as prominent figures in the Mahabharata epic, possess numerous alternative names (dasanama) that are rich in meaning. This study aims to describe and analyze the dasanama of Kresna and Arjuna in the Paparikan Bhagawadgita text using a semantic approach and uncover their underlying naming principles. Employing a qualitative descriptive method, this research uses a lontar manuscript of Paparikan Bhagawadgita from the collection of the Bali Provincial Center for Cultural Documentation and Preservation as its primary data source. Data consisting of words and phrases referring to both figures were collected through transliteration and translation, then analyzed etymologically to reveal underlying meanings. The findings reveal twelve dasanama, six for each character. Kresna's names include Harimūŕtti, Madhusūdana, Janārdana, Padmanābha, Keśawa, and Puruṣottama. Meanwhile, Arjuna's names include Pārtha, Kirithi, Dhanañjaya, Phalguṇa, Śwetawahana, and Mahābahu. These names derive their meanings from three naming bases: genealogical, characteristic, and historical-mythological. The findings demonstrate that the use of dasanama in the text is not arbitrary, but grounded in meanings tied to identity and background, providing deeper insight into literary characterization.
topic: Cultural and Religious Practices in Indonesia

title: Higher-Dimensional Consciousness Coupling Model (HDCM): A Theoretical Framework for Conscious Agency, Neural Implementation, and Cross-Dimensional Causation
abstract: The Higher-Dimensional Consciousness Coupling Model (HDCM) is a speculative theoretical framework for examining the relationship between conscious agency, neural implementation, and physical causation. The model distinguishes the observable neural state (B), the external physical world (W), a hypothesized conscious-subject state (H), and a coupling relation (C) between H and B. HDCM accepts the established dependence of conscious reports, perception, memory, and behavior on brain function, while examining whether neural dependence alone is sufficient to establish exhaustive neural generation of the conscious subject. A minimal dynamical formulation contrasts a neurally closed model with an alternative containing an additional coupling term. The framework further distinguishes an abstract higher-dimensional state space from the stronger hypothesis of an additional physical spatial dimension. It develops falsifiability criteria and discusses brain injury, memory, anesthesia, causal closure, conservation laws, death, and personal identity. This work does not claim that higher-dimensional life, souls, extra spatial dimensions, or post-mortem consciousness have been empirically demonstrated. These possibilities are treated as speculative interpretations whose scientific relevance depends on future testable predictions and evidence. Version 1.0. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22871648
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Trainee Dilemma: A Cultural-Historical Analysis of Transitioning From Student to Professional / El dilema del estudiante en practices: un análisis histórico-cultural de la transición entre estudiante y profesional
abstract: A critical phase in professional identity formation is the ‘trainee dilemma’. This dilemma marks the transition from formally qualified to a capable professional. During this period, individuals are qualified but not yet capable. Using concepts from Cultural-Historical Theory, we consider how the development of professional competence extends beyond formal education to include development of a new professional identity shaped by workplace experiences and interactions with senior colleagues. Formal educational achievements do not fully equip trainees for the practical demands of professional life. The workplace introduces new stimuli that require the integration of scientific and everyday concepts through experiential learning and social interaction. This analysis was developed drawing on the literature, interviews with professional educators, and our own research data. The concept of perezhivanie is central and used to show how transformative experiences are integrated into the trainee’s personality, reshaping their professional identity through impactful events and interactions. Measured support systems, such as mentorship and authentic tasks involving risk, are essential for fostering the trainee’s growth while providing safety nets to mitigate failures. Becoming a competent, confident, and committed professional is a transformative journey that not only enhances practical skills but also aligns the trainee’s professional and personal identities.

title: Consciousness, Survival, and Moral Accountability: Toward a Testable Science of the Afterlife
abstract: Chat GPT prompt: Include a short description of the essay for a Zenodo upload. Here is a concise Zenodo-ready description: This essay examines whether contemporary scientific evidence can support the hypothesis that consciousness survives biological death and that such survival could provide a mechanism for moral accountability. It reviews research on near-death experiences, cardiac arrest, reincarnation-type memories, terminal lucidity, mediumship, and consciousness science while distinguishing established findings from speculative interpretations. The essay proposes a speculative Continuity-Integration-Information (CII) hypothesis of consciousness and explores how future research—including Wolfram Physics, computational models, information theory, prospective resuscitation studies, and rigorous blinded experiments—could test hypotheses concerning personal survival and postmortem accountability. It also considers the philosophical and ethical conception of accountability discussed in Brian C. Muraresku and Karen Armstrong’s The GOD PARADOX. The essay does not claim that an afterlife has been scientifically demonstrated; instead, it proposes a falsifiable research program for investigating whether consciousness and personal identity could persist beyond biological death. title: An Ev5 Audit of Cartesian Recursive Consciousness
abstract: This independent research report applies Ev5 to two working papers by Walter Olinyk on Cartesian Recursive Consciousness (CRC). It examines what the papers’ philosophical arguments, constructed model, numerical diagnostics, and proposed interventions establish, and where further inferences remain necessary. The central analysis concerns the Perspectival Gap. In Paper 2’s worked example, the anticipated input distribution used to calculate the Gap score is specified separately from the running state update. Fixed-trajectory counterfactuals change that score without changing the model’s trajectory. The report also examines a tension between the paper’s non-reducibility condition and its worked distribution. These findings limit what the diagnostic demonstrates; they do not refute the possibility of an active anticipatory world relation. The audit also addresses Recursive Informational Closure, the Unity Point and spectral diagnostic, the proposed bridge from structure to lived perspective, human and artificial candidates, numerical identity, and welfare. It concludes that the papers offer a substantive research programme and a bounded mathematical demonstration, while claims about experience, personal identity, and moral status retain distinct evidential burdens. Reported simulation figures are attributed to Paper 2; the report’s counterfactual values are algebraic recalculations, not an independent simulation.

title: Ketika Self-Compassion Bertemu Peran Ayah: Kunci Regulasi Emosi Generasi Z di Karawang
abstract: Generation Z is deeply engaged with social media, which not only plays a role in the formation of personal identity but also serves as a significant source of emotional stress. This study aims to examine the influence of self-compassion and father involvement on emotional regulation among Generation Z in Karawang. A quantitative approach with a causal design was used in this study, which involved 204 participants. The research instruments used were the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ) to assess emotion regulation, the Self-Compassion Scale (SCS) to assess self-compassion, and the Reported Father Involvement Scale (FIS-R) to assess father involvement. The results of the simultaneous test showed a positive and significant effect (Sig. 0,000). Based on the positive unstandardized beta coefficients, it can be concluded that high levels of self-compassion and father involvement result in high levels of emotion regulation among Generation Z in Karawang. The overall effect size was 51,6%. The resulting, categorization indicates that self-compassion falls within the moderate range, father involvement within the low range, and emotion regulation within the high range. This study aims to deepen understanding of self-compassion and the role of fathers in fostering positive and adaptive emotional regulation among Generation Z.
venue: Reslaj Religion Education Social Laa Roiba Journal

title: Rewriting modernity: body, lepers, and the exoticizing gaze in Ma Yuan’s fiction
abstract: Abstract Ma Yuan’s fabrication (1986), widely regarded as one of the most challenging works of contemporary Chinese fiction, has been extensively analyzed as a quintessential example of metafictional writing. Departing from previous critics’ use of the term “meta-narrative,” this paper examines Ma Yuan’s experimental narrative as an exoticizing gaze that represents the bodies of lepers. Drawing on postcolonial theory and affect studies, I argue that this gaze marginalizes lepers as a minority Other within a Han-majority cultural context. Simultaneously, Ma Yuan idealizes Tibetans as embodiments of purity and benevolence while portraying them as traditional and pre-modern from a mainstream cultural lens. This dual representation, I propose, reflects Ma Yuan’s ambivalent stance toward socialist national discourses and the modernization process in post-Mao China. While attempting to rebel against authoritative ideologies, his narrative inadvertently reinforces dominant cultural paradigm. This tension highlights the broader challenges faced by Chinese avant-garde writers in the 1980s, who sought to redefine personal identity amidst the legacy of historical trauma while navigating the demands of sharing indigenous narratives within a globalizing cultural market during the reform era.

title: SOCIAL CLASS AND FEMALE IDENTITY IN JANE AUSTEN'S PRIDE AND PREJUDICE
abstract: The relationship between social class and female identity occupies a central position in Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice. Set within the hierarchical society of Regency England, the novel explores how women’s lives are shaped by class distinctions, economic limitations, family expectations, and marriage opportunities. This article investigates the ways in which social class influences the formation of female identity through the experiences of Elizabeth Bennet, Jane Bennet, Charlotte Lucas, Lydia Bennet, and Lady Catherine de Bourgh. Employing qualitative textual analysis, feminist literary criticism, and socio-historical approaches, the study examines how Austen portrays women’s attempts to negotiate personal desires within rigid social structures. The findings reveal that female identity in the novel is neither fixed nor solely determined by social position; rather, it emerges through the interaction of class, moral values, education, and individual agency. Austen challenges conventional assumptions regarding rank and respectability by demonstrating that genuine worth derives from character rather than inherited status. The article argues that Austen’s representation of women remains relevant because it highlights the enduring relationship between social structures and personal identity.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: From Fragmentation to Reparation
abstract: Kathleen O’Malley’s memoir, Childhood Interrupted, gives a powerful testimony of abuse that happened in Ireland’s industrial school system. The psychological effects of institutional abuse on the early development of a child have received less attention, despite the fact that current debates on such institutions frequently highlight historical and sociological viewpoints. This article looks at O’Malley’s narrative through the lens of Melanie Klein’s Object Relations Theory, with particular attention to the mechanisms of splitting, projective identification, and reparation. The argument is that the removal of the child from the maternal environment and the later incarceration in a punitive religious institution leads to a fragmented internal world where carers are internalized as persecutory objects, resulting in lasting feelings of shame, guilt, and mistrust. This study offers a detailed textual analysis of how institutional power derails early object relations and alters the child’s sense of self and capacity for relating. The act of reading the memoir itself can also be considered an act of belated restitution in which the survivor, by means of narrative reconstruction, is able to recompose fragmented memories and regain a sense of personal identity. The study contributes to cross-disciplinary discussions of childhood abuse, memory, and the long-term effects of authoritarian caregiving settings by focusing on the psychological dimensions of institutional trauma.
venue: The International Journal of Literary Humanities

title: Understanding the Needs of Siblings of Autistic Individuals and the Role of Online Community Support
abstract: People with autistic siblings often serve as informal caregivers from an early age, and might anticipate taking on a primary guardian role in the future. What are the unique needs of siblings, and what can be done to better support them? Could an online community help? This work aims to understand the experiences of people with autistic siblings through 12 semi-structured interviews with adults, and suggests designs for an online community tailored to them. We find that siblings’ lives have three primary phases: living at home with their autistic sibling, living independently, and potentially taking on a role as primary caretaker for their sibling. We focus on adults in the middle stage, who reflect on past and current support needs. A key challenge for community support environments is understanding how to allow an appropriate amount of venting, but prevent members from feeling overwhelmed by negativity. We present design recommendations for a lifelong online community that supports neurotypical siblings in balancing their personal identity with their evolving role as a caregiver, through life-stage sensitive and emotionally supportive interactions. Understanding the need for life-stage sensitive support in this demographic may provide insights into the need for life-stage-differentiated design for other groups.
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction

title: CROSS-CULTURAL ENCOUNTERS AND DIASPORIC IDENTITY IN THE FICTION OF JHUMPA LAHIRI AND KIRAN DESAI
authors: Jhili Patro,Dr. Sudipta Roy Chowdhury,Dr. Bail Kammari Rajya Lakshmi
abstract: The contemporary era of globalization has intensified migration and cultural exchange, making diasporic literature an important field for understanding identity, belonging, and cultural transformation. Among the most influential Indian diasporic writers, Jhumpa Lahiri and Kiran Desai explore the emotional, cultural, and psychological dimensions of migration through compelling narratives. Their novels and short stories portray characters negotiating between homeland traditions and host-country values while confronting issues of alienation, nostalgia, hybridity, and identity crises. This article examines cross-cultural encounters and diasporic identity in the fiction of Lahiri and Desai by analyzing selected works such as Interpreter of Maladies, The Namesake, and The Inheritance of Loss. Using a qualitative literary research methodology, the study highlights how both authors represent migration as a complex process involving cultural adaptation, intergenerational conflict, and the search for belonging. The findings reveal that while Lahiri emphasizes intimate family relationships and personal identity struggles, Desai focuses on globalization, postcolonial inequalities, and transnational experiences. Together, their works contribute significantly to contemporary diasporic discourse by illustrating the multifaceted realities of immigrant life. Keywords: Diaspora, Cross-cultural encounters, Identity, Migration, Hybridity, Jhumpa Lahiri, Kiran Desai, Globalization.
venue: International Journal of Economic Social Science and Management LAW

title: Youth well-becoming, leadership ability, and cultural identity in an educational program integrating cultural immersion, career mentorship, and advocacy training
abstract: Community-based youth development programs have the potential to promote youth self-efficacy and well-becoming while strengthening the communities in which they are embedded. Hyde Square Task Force (HSTF), a Boston-based organization established in the 1980s, supports Afro-Latin youth through arts-based cultural immersion, college and career mentorship, and opportunities for youth advocacy. Its flagship program, Jóvenes en Acción (JEA), serves students in grades 8–12 and places strong emphasis on the arts and community connection. In this study, we analyze qualitative and quantitative student feedback to assess the associations of JEA participation with youth identity development, cultural identity, career aspirations, skill building, capacity for advocacy, and sense of belonging. Our findings indicate that greater program participation and older age at participation are positively associated with scores in these domains, particularly participants' cultural and personal identity development. Results from free responses highlight the importance of trusted adult mentorship, culturally grounded arts programming, and inclusive community environments in fostering youth leadership and well-being. These findings support the value of integrated, arts-centered youth development models and offer insights for similar community-based programs.

title: Beyond Language Proficiency: Investigating Socio-Cultural Communication Practices in English Learning among University Students
abstract: Learning English in higher education has typically focused on the development of language competence. This study explored the socio-cultural communication in the English acquisition of university students, especially their negotiation of meaning, cultural identity building, responses to diversity and classroom communication adaptability. A qualitative study approach was adopted in an effort to explore the students' communication experiences in the real learning contexts in depth. Data were obtained through semi-structured interviews, classroom observations and document analysis. The results highlight the importance of socio-cultural elements in students’ English communication. Learners clarified, repeated, reworded, contextualized and adapted to overcome language and culture misinterpretations. The results indicate that students often employed local cultural experiences and personal identities as tools for meaning-making and participation in classroom activities. Collaborative educational activities, especially dyadic and group dialogs, offered an opportunity for learners to negotiate interpretations and to engage different perspectives. However, the document analysis showed that socio-cultural communication was not routinely specified as a clearly defined learning aim or assessment criterion. This study implies that English language training in higher education should go beyond the narrow focus on linguistic competence and systematically integrate socio-cultural communication into educational objectives, pedagogical strategies and assessment.

title: Obsessive-compulsive manifestations and rumination as predictors of body dissatisfaction in Spanish general population
abstract: Body image has become a central component of personal identity, especially in contexts where the value of appearance as an indicator of success predominates. Excessive preoccupation with the body is reminiscent of the dynamics of obsessive-compulsive disorder as the behaviour becomes ritualised. Rumination is repetitive thinking, focusing on the causes, consequences and symptoms of a negative feeling. The aim of this paper is to analyse how obsessive-compulsive symptoms and rumination contribute to body image concern in the general population taking into account gender. Methods. The sample consisted of 250 subjects (40.4% male), aged between 18 and 68 years with a mean age of 34.84 (SD = 13.33). A cross-sectional correlational design was used to study the associations between the different variables. Results. There is a positive relationship between obsessive-compulsive symptoms, rumination and the occurrence of body concerns. A stepwise regression analysis found that gender (β = .120, p = .021) together with obsessivity (β = .273, p = .001) and rumination (β = .355, p = .001) are the variables that best predict dysmorphic preoccupation and explained 29% of the variance. Conclusions. Rumination and trait obsessivity appear to be associated with dysmorphic symptoms in the general population and may be relevant factors to consider in future research on prevention and intervention.

title: CONTESTING LEGITIMACY AND PUBLIC IMAGE IN CORRUPTION DISCOURSE: AN ANALYSIS OF IMPOLITENESS STRATEGIES IN THE YAHAYA BELLO–EFCC MEDIA FACE-OFF
abstract: This study examines the impoliteness strategies deployed in the media confrontation between Yahaya Bello, former Governor of Kogi State, and the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) over allegations of financial misconduct. The study examines how both actors utilize impoliteness as a pragmatic resource for undermining credibility, defending institutional and personal identities, and negotiating legitimacy within Nigeria’s corruption discourse. Drawing on Culpeper’s Impoliteness Theory, Brown and Levinson’s Face Theory, and contemporary studies of media discourse, the study adopts a qualitative discourse-pragmatic approach to analyse selected media statements, press releases, and public responses related to the confrontation. Findings reveal the extensive deployment of bald-on-record impoliteness, negative impoliteness, ridicule, condescension, accusations, and associational impoliteness by both parties. The EFCC employs institutional accusations, public naming, and criminal labelling to undermine Bello’s public image and reinforce institutional authority. Conversely, Bello and his media representatives deploy counter-accusations, delegitimising descriptions, and victimhood narratives to challenge the anti-corruption agency's credibility and neutrality. The study concludes that impoliteness functions as a strategic communicative tool through which political actors and institutions negotiate power, legitimacy, accountability, and public perception in Nigeria’s corruption discourse.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Creativity and Expressive Contextualization in Gospel Songs in North-Central Nigeria: The Case of Idoma Gospel Songs
abstract: Among the Idoma people of north-central Nigeria, indigenous gospel music has become a popular means of worshipping God and of commenting on everyday life. Although these gospel songs draw themes from the Bible, they also draw on traditional expressive conventions to create a distinct musical genre that conveys the gospel message in ways consistent with Idoma cultural oral conventions, though originally unfamiliar in gospel music performance. They deploy unique communication skills that command audience attention and project self-assertion, privileging personal identity and relationship with God. One objective of this research is to uncover the traditionally unconventional creative styles of Idoma indigenous gospel artists. To do so, we examine two songs by Adams Onjefu, considered one of the foremost exponents of the Idoma indigenous gospel music genre. Observation, interviews, and analysis of this artiste’s recorded songs are the key instruments used to obtain data for this research. Some creative elements employed in Idoma indigenous gospel music include switching from singing to speech mode, the use of Corrective Confrontation (CC), and narrative mode in performances. Together, these demonstrate the artistry continuously engaged across different fora to convey both beauty and deeper understanding of concepts.

title: From “Woman in Chains” to Heroine: Feminism, Womanism, and Female Empowerment in Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s Devil on the Cross
abstract: This paper examines the representation of female assertiveness, feminism, and womanism in Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s Devil on the Cross. It focuses particularly on the protagonist, Jacinta Wariinga, whose experiences of sexual exploitation, economic marginalisation, patriarchal oppression, and social discrimination reflect the broader challenges confronting African women in a postcolonial society. Drawing on feminist and womanist theoretical perspectives, the study explores how Wariinga progresses from a vulnerable and oppressed woman to an assertive, economically independent, and self-conscious subject who challenges the structures that have historically subordinated women. The paper argues that Ngũgĩ presents Wariinga’s transformation as both a personal and political process, linking female emancipation to the larger struggle against capitalism, neo-colonialism, and patriarchy. Her reclamation of her body, labour, sexuality, and personal identity demonstrates the possibility of resistance and self-empowerment within an oppressive social order. The study further argues that the novel departs from conventional representations of African women as passive victims or symbols of tradition by positioning Wariinga as an active agent in the struggle for social transformation and national liberation. Ultimately, Devil on the Cross presents women’s emancipation as integral to the achievement of genuine Uhuru, suggesting that national liberation remains incomplete without the liberation and empowerment of African women.
venue: Aminu Kano Academic Scholars Association Multidisciplinary Journal

title: The Relatum Problem in Persistence: Why Identity Criteria Cannot Determine Their Own Domain
abstract: Metaphysical debates over diachronic identity are standardly structured around competing continuity criteria, systematically bracketing whether candidate bearers of identity are structurally authorized prior to evaluation. This paper argues that this oversight is not merely a benign pragmatic presupposition of inquiry, but a structural defect that systematically misconfigures past and present persistence debates. We establish the Relatum Authorization Necessity Thesis, demonstrating that persistence criteria presuppose relatum availability rather than generating their domains of application (V →C). To diagnose and correct this misconfiguration, we formulate the Diachronic Relatum Eligibility Framework (DREF). Rather than supplying a universal inventory of admissibility conditions or a new first-order theory, DREF constrains the order of justification by formalizing the dependency relation between admissibility conditions and relatum discrimination. By integrating framework-relative admissibility inventories via the Domain Eligibility Condition (DEC) where AT functions as a placeholder for explanatory constraints, adopting the Domain-Typed Applicability Lemma, and deploying personal identity variable disagreement (xorg vs. xpers) as our core diagnostic case study, this paper establishes a rigorous meta-theoretic requirement for diachronic metaphysics: before applying persistence criteria, establish the justificatory conditions under which a persistence question is well-formed.

These possibilities are treated as speculative interpretations whose scientific relevance depends on future testable predictions and evidence. Version 1.0. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22871648
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: This Is My Story (TIMS), a Five-Year Thematic Analysis of Patient Narratives from a Novel Intervention in an Academic Hospital
abstract: Background/Objective: This is My Story (TIMS) is a patient-centered, interview-based audio narrative program that provides a humanistic intervention to help the medical team understand more information about a patient’s story that is not routinely captured in their medical chart. The goal was to analyze themes present in the collected TIMS interview narratives and determine how they correspond to the specific interview prompts and discover whether there are any broader patterns and categories in responses. Methods: This is a secondary research study using retrospectively collected audio interviews, with hospitalized patients or their legally authorized representative, who provided their oral consent for the recording and future use of these interviews. A total of 362 TIMS interviews make up a subset of data for the reflexive thematic analysis, in which researchers analyzed, with some AI-assisted analysis, the themes that were present when the patient answered four structured interview questions. Results: The most common themes found were Experiences and Quality of Care, Family and Social Connections, Peace and Well-being, Joy and Meaning in Life, and Preferences and Personal Identity. Conclusions: The themes discovered in response to the four structured questions were directly related and influenced by the questions in which they correspond to, but there is also overlap between the questions, suggesting that each contributed to an overall cohesive patient narrative.

title: A STUDY OF HUMAN IDENTITY AND SOCIAL CONTROL IN THE DEPICTION OF DIGITAL DYSTOPIA IN ENGLISH NOVELS
abstract: The present study examines the depiction of human identity and social control in digital dystopia as represented in selected English novels. Digital dystopian literature explores the complex relationship between technological advancement, individual freedom, and institutional power in modern society. The study focuses on how digital surveillance, artificial intelligence, data collection, and technological dependence influence human identity, personal autonomy, privacy, and social relationships. It also analyses how powerful institutions use digital technologies to monitor behaviour, regulate social activities, manipulate information, and influence individual decisions. Special attention is given to the representation of characters who experience restrictions on freedom, challenges to personal identity, and conflicts between individual choices and technological authority. The study further examines literary techniques such as symbolism, imagery, characterisation, setting, and narrative structure through which authors present digitally controlled societies. A qualitative literary analysis is adopted to interpret the major themes and identify similarities and differences in the representation of digital dystopia. The study aims to demonstrate how English novels reflect contemporary concerns regarding technological power, ethical responsibility, privacy, and human agency. It also highlights the relevance of dystopian literature in understanding the possible social consequences of increasing dependence on digital technologies.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Intervention-Coverage Barrier: Why Finite Functional Tests Cannot Certify Neural Replacement Fidelity
abstract: Functional tests are indispensable for evaluating neural replacements, brain emulations, and other dynamical substitutes. A failed test can falsify fidelity at a declared interface, but success on a finite battery cannot by itself certify uniform fidelity over a continuous intervention domain.This paper formalizes an intervention-coverage barrier and separates three claims that are often compressed into the word "validation": finite-battery falsification, distributional validation under an explicit intervention law, and worst-case certification over a declared domain. It provides a constructive recurrent counterexample, a tight fill-distance audit under a sound global Lipschitz assumption, a dimensional lower bound, and the additional candidate-inclusive reachable-domain condition needed for recurrent transport.A frozen synthetic confirmation tested five parameterized recurrent packets. Across 368 trajectories and 3,632 tested state-input pairs, every candidate matched its source exactly on its finite battery but diverged by 0.12 to 0.20 at a reachable unseen intervention. Every sound one-step coverage audit rejected a 0.01 uniform certificate.This is a methods and theory preprint. It does not show that any specific neural replacement fails, that whole-brain emulation is impossible, or that consciousness, personal identity, survival, biological replaceability, or substrate independence is preserved or lost.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Answering “When Am I Ever Gonna Use This Again? Where Does This Come Up in the Real World?” Examining the Influence of University‐Community College Partnerships on Preservice Mathematics and Science Teachers and Faculty
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigated a research‐practice partnership (RPP) between a community college and university teacher preparation program that aimed to prepare secondary mathematics and science teachers to connect disciplinary content to authentic real‐world applications within their future high school classrooms. Data sources included multiple surveys, individual interviews, and focus group interviews with both faculty and preservice teachers across the RPP. Through participation in the partnership, preservice teachers gained knowledge of real‐world STEM applications, increased their awareness of career pathways, expanded disciplinary knowledge, modified their teaching dispositions, and built stronger connections with other participants. Faculty also reported expanded knowledge and networks, professional or personal identity development, and improved instructional practices. An initial RPP model is shared that illustrates a STEM Experiential Learning Experience implemented in the RPP. The initial model included the need to develop new knowledge, incorporate real‐world experiences, and emphasize classroom transfer. Findings indicated that additional components of career pathways, faculty impact, and teaching dispositions and community needed to be added to a revised RPP model. Implications included the need for constant communication, shared load, mutual buy‐in, and commitment to continuous learning from all members in an RPP.

title: THE LIMITS OF TECHNOLOGICAL HUMAN ENHANCEMENT A PHILOSOPHICAL AND ETHICAL CRITIQUE OF TRANSHUMANISM
abstract: This article presents a philosophical and ethical critique of transhumanism, with particular attention to projects aimed at radically enhancing the human body and mind through artificial intelligence, neurotechnology, implants, biotechnology, and human–machine integration. The study examines the main assumptions of transhumanist thought, including the belief that technological progress can overcome biological limitations, extend human life, increase cognitive capacities, and ultimately lead to the emergence of a posthuman form of existence. It argues that these promises are based on a reductionist understanding of the human person and insufficiently address the moral, social, political, and existential consequences of technological enhancement. The article introduces the concept of “destructive transhumanism” to describe forms of technological development that may undermine human autonomy, privacy, equality, personal identity, and responsibility. Particular attention is given to the risks associated with neurotechnologies, artificial intelligence, corporate control over human data, social inequality, and the gradual normalization of permanent technological intervention in the human body. The analysis does not reject therapeutic medicine or technologies designed to restore lost functions. Instead, it distinguishes medical treatment from enhancement projects aimed at creating a technologically superior human being. The article concludes that technological progress should remain subordinated to human dignity, ethical responsibility, democratic oversight, and the protection of fundamental rights.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Astrology and Relationship Compatibility: A Contemporary Perspective
abstract: Astrology has long been associated with the interpretation of interpersonal relationships, romantic compatibility, marriage prospects, and social interaction. In contemporary society, zodiac signs, birth charts, compatibility readings, and digital astrology platforms continue to influence how some individuals think about relationships. This paper examines astrology and relationship compatibility from a contemporary perspective, focusing on zodiac matching, birth charts, emotional compatibility, communication, marriage beliefs, self-reflection, digital astrology, cultural influences, and critical perspectives. Astrological compatibility may provide individuals with a symbolic language for discussing similarities and perceived differences between partners. It can also encourage conversations about personality, expectations, communication, and relationship preferences. However, relationship quality is influenced by many factors, including communication, trust, shared values, emotional maturity, social circumstances, and individual behaviour. Astrological compatibility should therefore be understood primarily as a cultural or reflective practice rather than a scientifically established predictor of relationship success. The paper argues that astrology remains socially relevant because it provides accessible narratives through which people discuss relationships and personal identity. A balanced contemporary perspective can recognize its cultural significance while encouraging evidence-based understanding of healthy relationships.

title: Rethinking The Study of Religion In Schools: Culture, Experience, and Educational Hermeneutics
abstract: This article reconsiders the place of religion in school education from a cultural-experiential and hermeneutical perspective. It argues that religion should be understood primarily as a human and socio-cultural phenomenon that plays a significant role in the search for meaning, the formation of personal identity, and the construction of life projects. Against this backdrop, the article critically examines the confessional approach traditionally associated with the study of religion, contending that its dependence on dogmatic presuppositions limits its capacity to respond adequately to the realities of religious pluralism within contemporary schools. Accordingly, this article argues that the study of religion in schools should be reconceived as a non-confessional, anthropological-hermeneutic discipline rooted in culture and human experience rather than in confessional transmission. In response to this need, the study proposes an educational hermeneutic grounded in an anthropological-hermeneutical framework that situates religion within the broader horizons of culture and lived experience rather than within the boundaries of particular faith traditions. Taking into account contemporary global transformations and emerging anthropological-cultural dynamics, the article advocates a non-confessional approach to the study of religion that is consistent with the educational identity of the school and the demands of pluralistic societies. It maintains that such an approach provides a more inclusive, pedagogically meaningful, and intellectually credible framework for engaging religious phenomena, while responding more effectively to the psychological, cultural, and social needs of students.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: THE ROLE OF @bts.bighitofficial INSTAGRAM REELS CONTENT IN SHAPING ARMY FAN LOYALTY IN EAST JAKARTA
abstract: The development of social media has transformed the pattern of communication between public figures and their fans. One of the most widely used features is Instagram Reels, which enables the delivery of information, entertainment, and interaction in a fast and engaging manner. This study aims to examine the role of Instagram Reels content on @bts.bighitofficial in shaping the loyalty of ARMY fans in East Jakarta. The study employs the Uses and Gratifications Theory, which views audiences as active users who utilize media to fulfill their needs for information, entertainment, social interaction, and personal identity. A descriptive qualitative approach was used, with informants selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, observation, documentation, and data triangulation. The informants consisted of three ARMY fans in East Jakarta who actively followed Reels content from the @bts.bighitofficial account. The findings reveal that BTS Reels content is characterized by informational, entertaining, and interactive content that fulfills fans’ needs. The study also found a high level of fan loyalty, demonstrated through active engagement in digital activities, support for BTS’s works, participation in fandom communities, and strong emotional attachment. Therefore, Instagram Reels content on @bts.bighitofficial plays a significant role in fulfilling fans’ needs and contributes to the development and maintenance of ARMY fan loyalty in East Jakarta.

title: Religious Understanding Transformation in Kitab Kuning Studies: A Phenomenological Study on Reflection, Internalization, and Social Praxis of Congregants
abstract: The study of yellow books at the grassroots level plays a strategic role in shaping Islamic literacy, but its dynamics are often reduced to the mere transfer of external knowledge. This study aims to explore in-depth the experiences of congregations in transforming religious understanding through the study of yellow books. This study uses a qualitative approach with a phenomenological design. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, participant observation, and documentation from two kyai and five congregations in Pemalang Regency, which were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The results show that 1) the transformation of religious understanding begins with cognitive disorientation towards classical texts, which is analyzed through the dialogical pedagogical mediation of the kyai; 2) the process of critical reflection and negotiation of meaning facilitates the internalization of values, where teachings are no longer viewed as external doctrines but are incorporated into personal identity; and 3) this internalization is manifested in a substantial increase in the quality of ritual worship, changes in patterns of social interaction to be more moderate and inclusive, and increased psychological resilience. This study concludes that the study of yellow books functions as a transformative catalyst that revitalizes the Islamic intellectual tradition to respond to the challenges of polarization. These findings offer a crucial bottom-up perspective for strengthening religious moderation and developing a reflective religious education curriculum.

title: When The Subject Disintegrates:
abstract: This study aims to rethink the human-centered tradition of social theory in light of posthumanist and relational ontologies. It argues that the foundational dualisms of modern thought—human/nature, subject/object, and society/technology—are increasingly inadequate for explaining contemporary socio-technical systems. By examining Latour's actor-network theory, Haraway's cyborg figure, Braidotti's conceptualizations of the posthuman and nomadic subject, and Verbeek's theory of mediation together, it is demonstrated that the concepts of agency, responsibility, and identity are distributed between humans and non-human entities. The text argues that technological objects function not only as instrumental entities but also as structures that transform social relations, ethical positions, and subjective experiences. In this context, personal identity, consciousness, or internal continuity is not a primary focus; rather, relational networks, material interfaces, and socio-technical mediations are considered (Parfit, 1975). Methodologically, the article adopts a critical-conceptual analysis, reading classical sociology, science and technology studies, and posthumanist literature in a comparative manner. Rather than making an empirical claim, it proposes an ontological and ethical expansion of sociological thought. Fundamentally, our assessment opens up a discussion on the possibilities of a sociological understanding that redefines responsibility in terms of boundaries, relationships, and mediations, rather than absolutizing the privileged position of humans in the social world.

title: My name is, who? On being misnamed by a relative or a romantic partner
abstract: The present survey investigated how people felt (i.e., irritated, sad or amused) when a relative or a romantic partner called them by someone else's first name. It also explored links between these reactions, self-esteem, the own name's symbolic value and one's own propensity to misnaming others. Participants reported more misnaming incidents committed by a relative than by a partner. Moreover, they were significantly more irritated when a partner misnamed them than when a relative did so. Globally, naming incidents did not trigger very strong negative feelings but participants reported correcting their interlocutor in a majority of incidents. Correlation analyses could only be performed on misnaming incidents committed by a relative, as incidents with partners were too infrequent. The intensity of feelings associated with these incidents were not predicted by self-esteem or the own name's symbolic value. However, resulting irritation was less intense and amusement stronger in participants who reported being themselves more prone to misnaming others. The link between people's metacognitive beliefs about their own naming abilities and the intensity of their feelings when they are misnamed is discussed. Finally, participants considered that the own name was a weaker symbol of personal identity than the own face. The advantage for the own face was nevertheless numerically small.

title: INVESTIGATING THE ROLE OF SOCIAL IDENTITY ON STUDENTS’ CLOTHING SELECTION PRACTICES IN ALVAN IKOKU FEDERAL UNIVERSITY OF EDUCATION
abstract: The study investigated the role of social identity on students’ clothing selection practices in Alvan Ikoku Federal University of Education Owerri, Imo State, Nigeria. Three purposes and three research questions were used for the study. Descriptive research design was used for the study. The population for the study was 2004 students comprising 1,295 third year students and 709 fourth year students from the six Schools in the University. Multi-stage sample technique was used to obtain a sample size of 210 students in stages. Instrument for data collection was questionnaire. The instrument was validated by three Home Economics lecturers from the Department of Home Economics and Hospitality Management AIFUE, Owerri. A reliability Coefficient of 0.85 was obtained. Data collected was analyzed using percentage. The results showed that the students’ clothing selection practices were influenced by their social group, social identity, personality, self-expression among others. The results also revealed that students use clothing to express and communicate their social and personal identity values and beliefs. Moreso, the study’s results indicated that there is a link between the type of clothing students select, wear and their character/behavior. The study concludes that informed decisions about students’ character and behavior can be observed and interpreted based on close observation on the students clothing selection and clothes they wear. The study recommends that workshops and seminars should be organized for staff on how students clothing selection practices can be linked to their personality, character and behavior.

title: Exploring College Students’ AI Dependence in Human–AI Collaborative Creation: Development and Validation of the CC-PACE Model
abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) poses significant challenges to creativity research and practice. Managing the degree of AI dependence during the creative process is therefore critical to fostering the healthy development of human creativity. To address this concern, this study proposes the CC-PACE model by integrating the 5A's framework with the I-PACE model, and examines factors associated with AI dependence during the creative process. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 813 college students in China, and the data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results showed that (1) both creative personal identity and creative self-efficacy were positively associated with closeness with the audience and the perception of AI as a creative agent. (2) Both closeness with the audience and the perception of AI as a creative agent were positively associated with time spent using AI, usage preference, and perceived difficulty in avoiding AI use. (3) Time spent and usage preference were positively associated with students' creative self-assessment, whereas perceived difficulty in avoiding AI use was not significantly associated with creative self-assessment. This study provides a viable analytical framework for understanding AI dependence in creative contexts. The findings further suggest that teachers should help students develop an appropriate understanding of AI's role, strengthen students' creative agency, and emphasize process-oriented assessment in creative activities.
